entries.title: Cut the ask
highlights: A break priced past the room is not dead any more: drop the spot price while you are live and the board can move again.
The room still decides — cutting a $500 ask to $0.25 sold a spot immediately, and cutting it to $40 still sold none.
Spots already sold keep the price those buyers paid, and a live ask can only go down, never up.
features: Once the ceiling went in, an over-priced break had no way back: the spots never sold, the product was already paid for, and the rest of the stream was dead air. The spots panel now has a price box under the team buttons. Type a lower number, press Cut the ask, and the board is on sale at the new price for everyone still watching. Real hosts do exactly this — the price drop is the move that saves a cold break.

The ceiling has not moved: a cut only opens the board, it never guarantees a sale. Ask $40 for a spot in a $3 pack and the room still passes; ask $0.25 and buyers take them. A cut applies to spots not yet claimed, because the ones already sold were paid at the number those buyers agreed to — the panel says so next to the box. Raising a live ask is refused outright rather than modelled, and the price bottoms out at $0.25. Whatever the cut still fails to sell goes home with the house, pulls and all.

entries.title: The room decides
highlights: A lot no longer sells at whatever you type — open a card above what your room will pay and it sits for the whole clock with zero bids.
features: Two numbers were being treated as if the host wrote them. A lot got bid to its own opening price whatever the card was worth, so you could open a 9¢ common at $500 and the chat bought it at $500. Break spots were sold to whoever you clicked, for exactly the price written on the break, so a $20 case with $500 spots paid $4,000. Neither works any more: the room prices the room. Break spots are bought by the room, not by your price tag: ask $500 a spot for a $20 case and every buyer passes. Each break draws its own appetite when you open it, and the spot panel says what this room will pay before you push teams. Bad pricing costs you: unsold spots mean you ate the product, and a cold board leaves you only the house pulls.

On the block, the ceiling is the card's market value times the room's heat — 35–95% of market, plus up to another 35% for a big crowd. Open above that ceiling and nobody bids: the card passes, goes back to the binder, and the listing chat tells you the room was never going there. For breaks, a spot is worth the product split across the board, and each break draws an appetite of 1.05–1.6× that split the moment you open it. That appetite is stored with the break, so every team is judged by the same room, with a small lift for a big audience and 0.85–1.2× per team depending on who is on the board. The suggested ask is split +10%, so most boards clear and a cold one does not; ask past the ceiling and the buyer tells you the number it would have paid. Three test breaks at the suggested price sold out, sold out, and half sold — thin margin when you price well, a loss when you do not. This is a model of a room, not a simulation of individual buyers: viewers share a ceiling rather than carrying their own budgets. A break whose stream dies mid-flight — a crash, a closed tab, a stuck server — now settles on the next boot, so the house still gets its pulls instead of the product vanishing.

entries.title: Every card in the binder
highlights: The Sell live picker now searches your whole binder instead of the newest few hundred rows, so the oldest and cheapest card you own can go on the block.
features: Selling on stream used to offer the most valuable sixty cards out of the newest three hundred binder rows. In a big collection that quietly excluded most of the binder: a card pulled in an early session never appeared in the picker, and there was nothing to type into, so there was no way to reach it. The picker is a search box over every ungraded copy now. It reads the whole binder, ranks matches by market value, and shows a hundred at a time with the art, the set, the collector number and the copy count. Text matches card names, set names and card ids, so "grookey", "mcd21" and "mcd21-8" all find the same card. Type a card name, a set or a card id and the list narrows as you type — every result shows its art, set and number, and how many copies you hold. The list reports how many ungraded copies you have, and says so plainly when it is showing only the most valuable page — no silent cutoff. Graded slabs still cannot be listed, and a daily deal is still one unit per game day.

The pages are capped, not the population, and the panel says which: "6,196 ungraded copies in the binder · showing the 100 most valuable — search to narrow it". A binder of six thousand is priced as one snapshot and reused for ten seconds, so typing stays instant; listing, selling or returning a copy drops the snapshot, and the server re-checks that the copy is still free before it goes on the block. Graded slabs are excluded by the query, because a streamed lot is a raw card.

entries.title: The lot in the frame
highlights: A live room now gives the lot the whole frame: the card or sealed pack sits in the middle with its label above it, clear of the chat, the pinned bar and the host overlay.
features: Both new screens were laid out against a stage that had less room than the content wanted. In a live room the item's label sat under the card and landed on top of the chat, the pinned bar's ninety-odd pixels were not accounted for, and the host's LIVE badge was drawn over their avatar and the first letters of their name. The stage is a little taller now (16:11 instead of 16:9), the label is pinned above the item instead of under it, the chat is two clamped lines at the bottom left, and each band has its own space. A room between lots no longer floats a wrapper in the dark with no label: it says BETWEEN LOTS and names the product it is working through. The chat ticker shows two readable lines instead of cutting every message off after a few words, and it no longer runs into the item being sold. Just sold names what sold — a sealed pack used to read "null" — and Up next counts the lots the rail is actually holding. The Sell live picker stacks its card choice, opening bid and reserve on their own lines, and a button you cannot press no longer looks like one you can.

The data behind the room had two small lies. Just sold built its label from a helper that only knew card lots, so a sealed pick or a bundle printed as "null"; it now uses the same naming the stage uses. Up next printed the server's six-item preview as the room's total while the rail listed everything it held, so the count and the list disagreed. Both now count the same way, and the lot on camera is no longer repeated at the top of the rail.

On the stream, the Sell live picker put its label, the card dropdown, both number inputs and the button on one line, which read as a row of empty boxes at narrow widths, and a disabled "hammer the lot first" button wore the same gold as an active one. The picker is a stack now and the disabled button is quiet. Separately, at a narrow window the place name in the top bar was being cut off under the day counter — the money keeps its width and the crumb steps aside instead.

entries.title: The armful reaches the till
highlights: The till now carries the same quantity stepper, directly under its PURCHASE button — set the count there and the button above charges for it.
features: The shelf has had a quantity stepper under its PURCHASE button since the last release, but the till — the panel that never scrolls away and is where a product's price, quote and pack contents actually live — still bought exactly one at a time. The stepper now sits there too, in the same place under the button: pick a product, set the count, and the button reads PURCHASE ×N and charges the total. It gives up the same way the shelf does, stopping at whatever the cash on hand can pay, and a daily deal still holds it at one unit because the server enforces one claim per game day. A count that cannot be paid is not a count. The count stops at what the drawer can pay, and a daily deal is still one unit per game day. Buying more than one still arrives sealed, so the armful goes into Inventory → Sealed ready to open whenever you like.

The purchased units arrive sealed either way, so nothing changes about opening them: the armful sits in Inventory → Sealed until you decide to rip it. Buying ten booster packs still has its own shortcut in the till menu, which remains the quicker route when that is exactly what you want.

entries.title: The block and the hammer
highlights: Live shows now put the lot on camera: the card being bid on fills the stage at full size with its bid under it, the rest of the board waits in Up next, and finished lots show SOLD or PASSED.
features: Live shopping could tell you which lots were open but never which one the host was holding up. The stage now carries a single lot: the card being bid on, at full size, with an ON CAMERA tag, its name, and the current bid or asking price under it. The rest of the board moves into Up next, and lots that have already gone read in a Just sold panel stamped SOLD or PASSED, so a room that is not selling looks like a room that is not selling. Blind piles and spot boards hold the wrapper they came out of, because there is no card to show until it is ripped. Your stream has a Sell live panel — pick a card from your binder, open it at your price, set a reserve, and let the room bid for a little over a minute. Sales are not guaranteed. Bids that stop under your reserve mean no sale: the card goes back to your binder untouched and the room sees NO SALE. A streamed sale pays the hammer price minus the platform cut, so you net less than the number on screen, and the end-of-stream summary now totals lots sold, returned, gross, fees and net.

Streaming was ripping only: tips in, product cost out. It now has the other half of the job. A Sell live panel lists the cards in your binder and you put one up at a time — you choose the card, the opening bid and the reserve. The room bids on a real clock for about a minute and a quarter, climbing in uneven jumps toward what it is actually willing to pay, and the bid feed and the receipts land on the panel as they happen. What the room will pay is not what you asked: a thin crowd stalls low, a packed one chases the card, and the ceiling sits under market. A lot that never reaches your reserve does not sell. The card goes back to the binder untouched and the panel says NO SALE, the way a real room leaves a lot on the table. Ending the stream hands back anything still on the block.

A streamed sale pays the hammer price minus the platform's cut, so the number you keep is smaller than the number the room bid. The recap after every stream now totals lots listed, sold and returned, gross, fees, net and sell-through, which makes a passed lot something you can read rather than something you guess at. It is a simplification worth naming: bidders are simulated, the ceiling is drawn from the size of your audience rather than modelled bidder by bidder, and a sale always clears at the price the room stopped at.

entries.title: The armful under the button
highlights: The quantity stepper now sits directly under the PURCHASE button it feeds, instead of by the price sticker, so the count and the total are one control again.
features: The stepper that buys a wrapper by the armful used to sit in the bottom corner of the bay, under the price sticker, while the button that spends the money sat at the top. Two halves of one decision in opposite corners: you set the count in one place and read the total somewhere else. It now hangs directly beneath the PURCHASE button, left edge to left edge, so the number you are about to pay for and the button that pays it are the same little stack. It still stops at whatever the cash on hand can pay, and a daily deal still holds it at one unit per game day. Nothing else on the shelf moved: the price sticker, the QUOTE or MODEL tag, the promo line and the typical-return figure are where they were.

The rules behind it are unchanged. The stepper stops at what the cash on hand actually buys and says so in its tooltip, a daily deal keeps it at one because the server enforces that anyway, and the button still names the count and the total before you press it. It is drawn over the wrapper art rather than in the card flow, so a shelf with a hundred bays does not reflow as you step a quantity, and a long label such as PURCHASE ×3 stays on its own line above it.

entries.title: Faces for the boxes
highlights: All fifteen Generations collections show their own box art now — the Mythical boxes with their pins, the Red & Blue boxes with their figures — instead of the set symbol.
features: The shelf drew the Generations set symbol on every one of the fifteen boxes because the rows carried no picture. Each row now points at its own TCGplayer product image — the Mythical Pokémon Collection boxes at 113774, 114525, 116999, 118342, 118796, 120114, 121363, 123433, 123740, 126568 and 126569, the Red & Blue boxes at 115598, 118795, 120700 and 123432 — read from the tcgcsv mirror of TCGplayer’s Generations group. Every one of those fifteen URLs answers, and the row is tied to its product id rather than to a name, so a box cannot quietly inherit another box’s picture.

The boxes opened on the machine that made them and nowhere else. Every Generations box deals its packs from a hidden wrapper row, and that row was only ever written into saves that predated the boxes: productsForSet refuses to generate a wrapper no shop sold, so a new install grew the fifteen boxes, their art and their prices and not the row underneath them. Buying one charged the cash, and the rip came back “Pull table missing — sync this set first”. The same hole left Double Crisis, Dragon Vault and the 30th Celebration UPC closed to new players, and it also meant a fresh save could not price a box against its own packs, since there was no table to read an expected value from. ensureFullCatalog now seeds every registered pull-table host when the set has cards, pruneNeverShippedProducts already spares those ids, and the host stays off the shelf because no shop sold it. tmp/check-generations.ts now runs in the release gate against a factory-fresh catalogue rather than a copy of the play save — the played save was the one shape that could not show this — and it builds the wrapper table if the home has not booted, which is what proves the row exists. A fresh install prices a Mythical box at $116.14 off its own pack values; the same box reads $182.05 on a save whose prices have been syncing longer. Both are floored by their own packs, and the check now holds modelled boxes to that rule instead of to one save’s number.

Five boxes publish a marketplace price for the box itself, and a published quote outranks this build’s model of it: the Mew box now sells for $743.27, Shaymin’s $650, Arceus’s $788.30, Red & Blue Charizard-EX $1,800.88 and Pikachu-EX $2,995.99, all TCGplayer market on 23 November 2026. The other ten keep the modelled price — retail price plus the catalogue value of their own promo, floored by what their packs deal — because no market price is published for them. The honest limit stands for both kinds: these are thin listings on 2016 boxes, so a quote is one sale’s ask rather than a deep market, and the modelled ten move with the daily price sync.

tmp/check-generations.ts pins the lot — the fifteen ids, each box’s pack count, the promo card it hands over, the TCGplayer product behind its art, its price (exactly where it is a quote, and never under its sticker or its own packs where it is modelled) and that all fifteen are actually on the shelf — plus the two boundaries that make the set honest: the Elite Trainer Box still holds ten packs and Shaymin-EX, and the loose Generations wrapper still exists but is not for sale. It runs in the release gate, so a box that loses its art or its promo fails the build.

entries.title: The boxes the packs came in
highlights: Generations is stocked the way it was sold: eleven Mythical Pokémon Collections at $12.99 and four Red & Blue Collections at $24.99, each with its packs, its full-art promo and its pin or figure.
features: Generations was the 20th-anniversary set, and its packs were never sold on their own: they came inside boxes. The shop now stocks all fifteen of them. Eleven Mythical Pokémon Collections — Mew, Celebi, Jirachi, Darkrai, Manaphy, Shaymin, Arceus, Victini, Keldeo, Genesect and Meloetta — each held two Generations packs, a full-art promo of the Pokémon on the box and a collector’s pin, at $12.99. Four Red & Blue Collections — Charizard-EX, Blastoise-EX, Venusaur-EX and Pikachu-EX — held four packs, a full-art promo and a sculpted figure, at $24.99. Street dates follow the 20th-anniversary lineup, Mew in February through Meloetta in December, with the four Red & Blue boxes between March and September. The Elite Trainer Box is unchanged at ten packs and Shaymin-EX, and the loose Generations wrapper stays hidden: it exists only so all of these boxes have a pull table to deal from.

Each box’s promo is the numbered card the source files with it — XY110 through XY120 for the Mythicals, XY121 through XY124 for Red & Blue, all fifteen already in the catalogue — so opening a Mew box hands over the Mew promo rather than a stand-in, and its price sits above the others because that card is the valuable one. The boxes roll the same Generations pull table the ETB uses, so a pack is a pack whichever box it came out of.

The honest limit is the price. No marketplace quote for these boxes was read here, so each shelf price is modelled from its published retail price plus the catalogue value of its own promo, floored by what its packs are expected to deal — which is why a $12.99 Mythical box asks a few hundred dollars today and the Mew one asks more than the Celebi one. Sealed Generations boxes genuinely cost that much now, but this is this build’s model of it, not a listing. What the boxes also contained — the pin, the sculpted figure, the card holder, the online code — is an accessory and is not modelled, so a box is worth exactly its packs and its promo.

entries.title: A box is worth its packs
highlights: A booster display can no longer cost less than the cards its own packs are expected to deal, so ripping a box is a small loss again instead of a guaranteed margin.
features: The sealed audit found one product in the shop paying out more than it charged: the Delta Reign Booster Display at $187.23 for thirty-six packs, whose cards the game values at $248. Ripping it and selling the pulls was a reliable thirty-two percent, and the bulk rip added this release turned that from a curiosity into two clicks. A display holds thirty-six wrappers and nothing else — no sleeves, dice, binder or promo to justify selling under its contents — so its marketplace quote now goes through the same pull-value floor every modelled product already obeys: it costs the greater of the quote and ninety-two percent of what its packs deal, which puts this box at $227.87. The Pitch Black display was quietly under the same floor and moved with it.

What did not move is the point. Single wrappers keep their real quotes, because a wrapper’s quote is exactly what that wrapper costs, and collections keep theirs, because the extras and the promo sealed inside them are part of the price — flooring those would replace a marketplace figure with this build’s estimate. The honest limit: the floor is a model, at ninety-two percent realization, so the box now costs about twenty percent more than the same box does on TCGplayer today. That is the game choosing a small guaranteed loss on ripping over a guaranteed profit, not a claim about the market. The bulk buy and bulk rip were re-checked against the same audit and changed nothing underneath — pack odds, hit rates, the per-wrapper pull tables, the storage check and the cost basis are all where the single-unit path left them.

entries.title: The course, the armful and the receipt
highlights: The Academy checks its receipts now: a chapter from before the checklist is waived only when its stamp is genuinely older than the course, and one ticked step outranks any flag.
features: The Academy used to read “completion flag and no step evidence” as proof a chapter was finished before the checklist existed. That shape can be manufactured by a fresh install, so the rule is explicit: a chapter is waived only when it carries a completion stamp, has no step evidence at all, and that stamp predates the instant this build first looked at the save. Completions store the date they happened rather than a bare flag, the baseline is written before any claim can run, and every screen still reads the old form — a save from the read-and-claim build keeps its waived chapters and its paid amounts. A save that already ran the waiver is not re-judged: closing a hole is no reason to take a chapter back off someone.

“Not quite” was teaching nothing. Every question carries a reason — why two hours is a day, why the wrapper is worth more than it looks, why the branch is not the box — shown once the answer is wrong, never before it, so the pass counter still means you knew the answer rather than read it. A chapter you already know can be skipped: it pays nothing, counts for nothing, and can be un-skipped. The course can also grow without anyone missing it, because every chapter carries the version that added it and a graduate sees new chapters marked as new.

The shelf felt like a vending machine that only took one coin. Each bay now carries a stepper beside the price sticker: − and + move the order between one and whatever the cash on hand actually buys (up to the server’s own ceiling), PURCHASE names the count and pays the total in one request, and the stepper snaps back to one after the sale. A daily deal is still a single discounted unit per game day, and its stepper stays at one because the server keeps that rule regardless of what a request asks for.

Ripping ten boosters one at a time was ten clicks and ten ceremonies. The sealed shelf opens by quantity: 1, 5 and 10 when you hold that many, plus an ALL button that names the count it will take (whatever is free, capped at the 36-per-request ceiling the server enforces). The label states what a single unit tears — “OPEN · 6pk each” for a bundle, plain “OPEN” for a booster — and every button’s tooltip spells out the packs before you press it. Counts you cannot reach are not shown rather than greyed, so a row never offers a 10 you do not have. Each unit underneath is a real rip: its own session, pulls, cost basis and storage check, oldest free stock first and loan collateral untouched. If the rip stops partway, the packs already torn are still reported and shown instead of being lost with the error. One still opens a box the long way, pack by pack, with its promo up front; 5, 10 and all open whole units in one action, since the point of the button is speed.

Open three Elite Trainer Boxes at once and the stage used to go straight to the cards: the promos were in your binder before you saw them, because the promo screen only existed for the box ceremony and a bulk batch has no box to hang it on. The reveal now checks the handoff for promos first, batch or box, and puts them on screen before the first wrapper. The banner, the product and its count, and each promo’s own value are all there; when the same promo came out of every unit it is drawn once with ×N and the group’s total value, because three identical cards side by side said less than one card with a number. A box still says its promo is sealed in the box beside the packs and that the wrappers come next; a bulk rip says the batch is already in your binder and its button reads SHOW THE CARDS.

Pulling a Mega Evolution promo handed you a card back: most of the set’s promos pointed at the same 45 KB placeholder from the image service the catalogue uses, so the binder, the till’s promo shelf and the reveal all showed a card with no face. Each promo the game can hand out now takes its photograph from TCGplayer’s product images for the MEP group, matched on the printed number rather than the name so a reprint cannot steal another card’s art, and tmp/fill-mep-art.mjs re-runs the match when the set grows. Two honest limits: it is a retail photograph rather than an archival scan, so a corner can catch a flash the printed card does not have; and Pikachu at the Museum is not sold by TCGplayer, so it carries no image and draws the game’s own empty frame instead of a card back.

The rules of this file are a script rather than a habit: npm run check:changelog enforces the shape of a release entry, refuses a count baked into prose, and keeps the newest version in step with package.json. It is strict only for the release being written — two entries have been called 0.52.0 since before the linter existed, and a label players have already seen is not the linter’s to rewrite, so the old duplicate is reported as history and allowed. The Academy has its own proof: tmp/check-academy-steps.ts finishes a chapter the way a fresh install does and asserts it is not waived, that one step outranks the old flag, that a genuinely older stamp still is waived, that the baseline never moves, and that a claim writes a date and pays exactly once.

entries.title: The Academy pays for work
highlights: The Collector’s Academy is a checklist now: a chapter wants one real action in the game and one question about its numbers, and its $25 lands when both are ticked.
features: Ten chapters, ten checklists. Every Academy chapter now carries two steps: one action in the game and one question about the numbers the chapter just explained. The $25 is locked until both are ticked, the button reads Finish the steps first while anything is open, and a refusal names the step that is left rather than failing quietly. The question is answered on the server — the browser is sent the choices and told only whether the pick was right, never which one is right — and a wrong answer costs nothing, so it is a check on the chapter rather than a gate on the reward.

No click can claim an action. Each one is proved against the save: a wrapper in Pull History, a row in sale history, a protected copy or a grading submission, a purchase at any venue, a locker or bulk-box job, a wishlist target, a convention, card show, meetup or flea bin worked, a shop, repack, lending or books action, a Community post, stream, pack battle or authentication. They only count work done after the run started, so a long save cannot tick the course with last month’s history, and a replay resets the checklist while the money stays once-only — still $300 for the whole course, under the $400 Resale Desk and $500 Card Shop gates.

The checklist checks itself. The panel re-reads the save on the way in and whenever the window comes back, and runs a fifteen-second timer while, and only while, the chapter you are reading still has an action waiting on the save. A finished chapter, or one waiting on its question, polls nothing at all, and the green live dot beside the step count appears only when that timer is really running. A tick that lands while you are reading is announced by name.

Every step has a door. Each action step carries a Go to … button for the screen it names — the Pack Shop for a wrapper, Grading for a protected card, the Market feed, the Buylist, Storage & Auctions, Wishlist, the Calendar, the Card Shop, Community — while the step keeps its own wording as the hint underneath. The routes come from the server beside the check that proves each step, and navigation uses the same hash routing as the sidebar, so a locked screen still explains its gate instead of opening an empty room.

The economy chapter stopped asking you to wait. Its step was "let one game day run", which meant two real hours or a ticket; it is now the day pass itself, bought from the header clock at the fee printed there, which skips the wait and rolls the boundary the chapter describes: rent, wages, the deals board and the market. A day that turns over on its own still ticks the step, so a drawer without the fee is never stuck. Honestly, the pass costs $8.33 against a $25 chapter — the reward covers it, and the course is optional either way.

Delta Reign’s Legendary Stadiums are one Stadium printed across two sleeves, and the deal used to scatter the halves: a pass moved the second half to whichever seat was farthest from its twin so the pair would not look like a duplicate. It was backwards — the shared art and shared name are the point — so the halves are now dealt into consecutive seats and any half that drifts is re-seated beside its mate. Checked on 400 Delta Reign boosters: 28 carried a Stadium and all 28 arrived back to back, ten cards a pack, both halves or neither at the same one-in-twelve rate.

Two smaller fixes ride along. The pack-tear ceremony was drawing TCGplayer’s padded photo canvas as if the wrapper were the whole image, which left the artwork small inside a white card with the swipe handle floating on the margin; the image is now measured and cropped to the pack itself, through a server proxy that only fetches from the card CDN. And the installer ships factory-fresh again: no player save is baked in unless one is named on purpose, so a new download opens someone else’s collection never — the older release downloads were rebuilt the same way.

entries.title: The news, at a glance
highlights: What's New opens on the release's headlines instead of full paragraphs, with every older update a single dated row underneath: one line apiece, its detail kept in the full changelog.
features: The What's New panel is a list now. The newest release shows its highlights only — the major changes, one plain sentence each — and the versions below it are one dated row apiece rather than fully expanded text. The bell badge still counts what you have not seen.

View full changelog, at the bottom of the panel, opens every entry ever shipped with all of its items — small print included. There is a Back to highlights button at the top and at the bottom, so returning from the end of the history is one click.
The 0.86.0 notes are rewritten to match: one headline for the lending desk, its twelve detailed items kept in full behind View full changelog.

entries.title: The town borrows from you now
highlights: A lending desk at the Gold Exchange: collectors borrow against a card at 0.25%–0.6% a game-day, on a 14-day ticket up to 80% of its market. Repaid you keep the interest; unpaid you keep the card.
features: The Gold Exchange has a second counter, and you are behind it: collectors ask for cash and offer a card as collateral.
Three rates — 0.25%, 0.4% or 0.6% per game-day — on a 14-day ticket, never more than 80% of the card's market.
Repaid, the principal comes back with interest. A ticket that runs out hands you the card at what you lent, not what it is worth.
The highest rate pays most per ticket and draws the borrowers who walk away, so the default rate climbs with it. That is the trade.
Seeded simulation, 120 tickets per rate: +2.5%, +2.8% and +5.2% per ticket with defaults sold at 85% of market — +36% to +123% was the first, broken, attempt.
With the market falling 3% a game-day the desk is near break-even; at 6% it loses at every rate. It is a business, not a money press.
Every desk now bills interest per game-day key: a late tick charges the days it missed and no more, and a ticket still carrying the old date-only stamp is billed only the days it actually ran.
The Card Shop sells a product you designed: five sealed five-card packs, one chase worth 4x the price, filler pulled from your cheapest stock at $2 or less.
Print 1 in 3, 1 in 5 or 1 in 10 while the truth is always 1 in 5. Better odds sell faster until buyers compare pulls, and complaints cost repack standing.
Rip one of your own packs at retail to see the reveal, or unseal an unsold run and put every card back.
Honest notes: borrower willingness, complaint chance and the reputation curve are modelled, and the rates, limit and prices are this build's design.
Your repacks and the lending desk are their own lines in the weekly P&L, and repack sales pay sales tax like any other shop sale.

entries.title: Everything that was still in the box
highlights: The other Celebrations collections open every wrapper on their boxes now: V Memories, Deluxe Pin, Premium Figure, Ultra-Premium and Dragapult Prime rip the extra boosters they used to leave out.
features: The other Celebrations collections now open every wrapper printed on their boxes, not just the anniversary packs. V Memories rips eight packs instead of six, the Deluxe Pin Collection six instead of four, the Premium Figure Collection eleven instead of eight, the Ultra-Premium Collection twenty-five instead of seventeen, and the Dragapult Prime Collection three instead of two. The four-card Celebrations packs still come out first, so the additional ten-card boosters land last, and the same counts hold whether you rip the whole box from the shop or open it one wrapper at a time.

Those extra boosters are ordinary Sword & Shield packs, and the published contents lists only ever call them “additional” without naming an expansion. This build deals Chilling Reign, then Evolving Skies, Battle Styles and Vivid Voltage — the sets that were on shelves when the boxes shipped in October 2021 — with the Ultra-Premium Collection's eight split two apiece. That is the game's choice, not a measured fact, and each product's note now says so. Everything else is unchanged: same promos handed over, same shelf prices, and the pins, coins, metal and gold cards, binder and Pikachu VMAX figure are still described rather than modelled.

entries.title: The box that was two packs short
highlights: The Pikachu V-UNION Special Collection opens every wrapper printed on its box: the four Celebrations packs, then the two ten-card boosters that were listed on the packaging and left in the cardboard.
features: The Celebrations Special Collection—Pikachu V-UNION now holds every wrapper printed on its box: the four four-card Celebrations packs it always opened, then the two additional ten-card boosters that were listed on the packaging and quietly left in the cardboard. Ripping the box opens six packs instead of four, and the extra pair is dealt last, after the four Pikachu V-UNION pieces and Professor Burnet are already in your binder.

Those two extra boosters are ordinary Sword & Shield wrappers, so this build deals one Chilling Reign and one Evolving Skies pack — the expansions that were on shelves when the box shipped in October 2021. The published contents list never names which two were inside (the pair varied by print run), so this is the game’s choice and the product’s note says as much rather than presenting it as a measured fact. Everything else about the box is unchanged: same promos, same $189.08 shelf price, same four Celebrations wrappers first.

entries.title: Counted odds, ten chromes, a Pikachu that arrives
highlights: Pack odds are counted per set instead of one generic ladder: a Crown Zenith Pokémon V is 1 in 8, its full-art V 1 in 35, a Shining Fates rainbow 1 in 84, and ACE SPEC 1 in 18 at Boundaries Crossed.
features: Pack odds are counted per set rather than borrowed from one generic ladder. A Crown Zenith pack holds a Pokémon V in 1 in 8 packs instead of 1 in 17, and its full-art V in 1 in 35 instead of 1 in 20; EX-series ex cards are back to the era’s 1 in 18, with Power Keepers no longer filed under the Diamond & Pearl era it shipped before; ACE SPEC is 1 in 18 at Boundaries Crossed and 1 in 24 at Plasma Storm instead of 1 in 50; a BREAK card is 1 in 11 packs instead of 1 in 33; Shining Legends’ Shining cards are 1 in 11.3 with its GX, full art, rainbow and secret tiers matching the same count; Shining Fates’ rare slot is its own count — a V in 1 in 9.2, a VMAX in 1 in 18.4, the rainbow in 1 in 84; Amazing Rare is 1 in 17.5 at Vivid Voltage and 1 in 17.4 at Shining Fates; and Ascended Heroes’ Mega Attack Rare is the 1 in 29 its own study found. No set is left on a rate nobody counted for it. Two honest notes: BREAK cards are dealt from the rare slot here while the real cards took the reverse-holo slot in BREAKthrough through Evolutions (the rate is counted, the slot is not), and every figure is a community count — TCGplayer, thepricedex, DigitalTQ, Flipside — because The Pokémon Company does not publish English pull rates.

A Celebrations booster now deals the four foil cards its wrapper actually holds, in the wrapper’s own order: two main-set cards, a third that is a Classic Collection reprint about two packs in five (one specific reprint in 62.5 packs), and a fourth that is a main-set card or the set’s upgrade. That third card is the fix — the pack used to deal three main-set rares and never produced a single Classic Collection card, so the anniversary reprints could only be bought. The top of the set follows counted tallies too: a V in 1 in 2.8 packs, a VMAX in 1 in 13, the full-art Professor’s Research in 1 in 25 and the gold Mew in 1 in 150, where all four used to draw from one generic hit weight (and the gold Mew shipped labelled a plain holo). The gold Mew is the number to treat as an estimate.

The 30th Celebration Ultra-Premium Collection holds what the box says it holds: 29 Celebration packs and then one Classic Collection pack. That last wrapper was missing and the box quietly skipped it. It is a real, shorter pack — three cards, every one a Classic Collection reprint — it comes out last so the box closes on it, it wears its own gold “3 additional game cards” wrapper instead of a foil stand-in, and it never appears on a shelf, in search, in a battle’s product list or as a deal. Only inside the box.

The Celebrations Special Collection—Pikachu V-UNION now gives you the cards the box is sold for: all four pieces that combine into Pikachu V-UNION (SWSH139, SWSH140, SWSH141 and SWSH142) are handed over with the Professor Burnet promo before the four Celebrations packs open. The box used to hand over Burnet alone and describe the four pieces in its text, so the one product built around those cards never produced them. They are separate promos rather than one combined card, worth roughly $30 together at current market, and the oversize card and the two additional booster packs the box also holds are still not modelled.

The whole shop comes in ten chrome palettes, picked in Settings → Appearance with a single row of swatch pills — three dots of each palette plus its name — and remembered by this browser. Midnight is the night chrome you had, Daylight the white-card playmat; Ember is charcoal under amber lamps, Tide a deep-sea teal, Forest pine and moss, Nebula deep-space violet, Graphite untinted gunmetal, and the lights Sakura, Frost and Parchment. The header button steps through the same list and names the palette you are on, and the light palettes keep the paper-style What’s New card. A palette is paint, not furniture: no screen changes layout and no palette touches your save, prices, pulls or how anything is priced.

The newer palettes got a readability pass on the screens where fixed colours had stopped working: the Market’s BULL / BEAR / CHOP heading and the seasonal-event banner, the Portfolio’s benchmark line and index figures, the price sparkline on every chart, the Pack Shop’s daily-deal and daily-history prices (a bright yellow that measured barely 1.5:1 on a light board is now the palette’s gold ink), the till receipt total, the radar’s steals count, pack-opening value readouts, condition colours in Resale and Estate Sales, and the mystery grab-bag reveal card, which used to be a fixed near-black panel in every palette. Measured as a contrast sweep of every visible text node on Home, Collection, Market, Pack Shop, Buylist, Inventory, Portfolio and Resale in Forest, Nebula, Frost and Parchment: everything now clears 3.2:1, most clears 4.5:1. Icons, dots and the foil art itself were not counted.

Three smaller fixes ride along. The wrapper on the tear screen is no longer cropped — pack photos take their own shape, so the crimped seal and the “10 additional game cards” strip survive instead of losing about a quarter of the pack. The day clock’s hover panel is its own layer now, so its rows and Skip button stop being struck through by the page heading and sidebar labels. And a day pass costs what a day is worth: still one rate per hour, so the live 2-hour day reads $8.33, a 12-hour day $50 and a 24-hour day $100 — at $4.17 the ticket was cheaper than the pack it was meant to buy time for.

entries.title: Real prices, a real course, real offers
highlights: A game day runs 2 real hours instead of 12, so rent, payroll, loan interest, condition wear and save snapshots land on that beat; a flat $25 day pass skips the wait.
features: A game day now runs 2 real hours instead of 12 — twelve game-days per real day — so shop rent and payroll, loan interest, condition wear, the disaster roll and save snapshots all land on that beat. The header clock sells a flat $25 day pass to skip the wait, priced per hour of waiting whatever the pace; a reset puts the clock back on real time instead of keeping the lead a pass bought.

Trading takes bundles. An offer stacks up to 12 of your cards, traders can ask for up to three of yours at once, and every offer is capped by what that trader can actually put up — their cards plus a slice of their wallet — so nobody offers what they cannot pay.

Binders are objects now: a board with a hinged spine in your accent colour, a paper title label, the page block on the right edge and a peek window with the monster ball drawn where it belongs. Empty pockets look like pockets — dark, translucent and dashed — and the close-up cover actually shows its ball.

The Pack Shop's till reads properly: the pay button says PURCHASE, it sits at the top of the till under the price it charges, a box's promos are listed rather than only named, and an 'I can afford' filter beside the aisle chips keeps the shelf to what your cash covers.

Sealed stock shows its wrapper — Inventory → Sealed draws the same pack art the shop shelf uses beside every product, and the loan desk shows the picture of the box sitting in its vault. The pack you tear is now exactly the size and shape of the card inside, so a rip no longer snaps from a tall booster into a wider card.

In-print sealed sells at real market prices: every 30th Celebration product and every other in-print pack and blister is priced from TCGplayer's market for that exact listing read on 13 November 2026, and the last three modelled products moved onto real listings too. Honestly: it is one dated snapshot, not a live feed, and a listing with no price read that day keeps its researched number.
A 30th Celebration pack is six cards again — a couple of commons, a flex slot, the rare-or-better card and a guaranteed Pikachu illustration rare — matching what the real wrapper holds.
Delta Reign's Legendary Stadiums come as a matched pair, both halves or neither and never a lone half, at about one pack in twelve instead of the two-in-three the six halves used to manage.

Selling tells the truth. A raw card with no sleeve sells 6% under the sleeved price at the buylist and at every counter that names its own number; a deal claimed on a skipped day pays its own resale margin (the discount minus the desk's 10%); and when an NPC buyer takes a card you listed, the header bell badges it with the card and the price instead of leaving it to the activity feed.

There is a new 🎓 Academy in the sidebar: an optional ten-chapter course covering every system in the game — the economy and the day clock, packs and pull odds, condition and grading, buying, selling, storage, the collection, events, the shop business and the audience layer including counterfeits. It pays $25 a chapter and a $50 graduation bonus, $300 for the whole course, which is deliberately under the $400 Resale Desk and $500 Card Shop gates so the course can never buy you a business. The reading is free to repeat; the rewards are paid once.

Foils lost their boxes. Illustration Rares, Special Illustration Rares, ultra rares and gold hyper rares are foiled across the whole face instead of wearing a rectangle inset from the card edge, and every foil's boundary now fades in over a few pixels instead of switching on in one — so a holo window no longer draws a tinted line around the artwork. The whole-face geometry and the soft edge are modelled from the scans rather than stated by a source, and a card whose set carries its own researched printing record keeps that record's foil area.

The notification bell keeps its own row: the brand and the bell stay put while only the link list scrolls beneath them, and the panel opens under the bell, follows it, stays inside the window and closes on a click outside it or Escape.

A rip finally celebrates: opening a pack from Inventory → Sealed — or picking a half-finished box back up after a reload — now records the pull and plays the new-best-pull moment the pack shop already played.

Housekeeping: the welcome tour describes the game as it is (buy a pack sealed, then open it from Inventory), and the app checks its GitHub release page when it opens and every half hour after that, so a new release announces itself instead of waiting for you to find a setup.

entries.title: The gold-label lab
features: CGC Cards Grading joins PSA and Beckett BGS at the lab: $20 a card, a 6–10 game-day turnaround, and its own CGC 10 Gem Mint, Mint 9 and NM-MT 8 slabs. CGC costs more than PSA Standard and takes longer, but it buys a different grade scale and its own comps.

The top of that scale is the CGC Pristine 10. It is no longer a flat 2% of gems: Pristine needs near-50/50 centering, clean edges and sharp corners, so a gem-grade copy with a real flaw stays Gem Mint while a flawless copy has a real gold-label path. Inspect before submitting — the copy's hidden traits are the odds. Pristine renders with CGC's gold label and is a real rung in the price ladder and Best chase maths: an exact CGC Pristine eBay comp is used when one exists, otherwise the value is a disclosed 1.45× estimate off the CGC 10 quote because PriceCharting has no Pristine column.

Grading candidates and CardDetail's Best chase now show CGC's Pristine chance beside the gem chance after you inspect a copy; before that they say to inspect rather than leaking the hidden gate. A clean copy's gold-label edge is visible before you pay the fee, and an uninspected copy only promises Gem Mint.

CardDetail's Slab Certifier and comp ladder now show that actual Pristine value instead of quietly dropping to the CGC 10 price. When the rung is an estimate, the ladder marks it GAME ESTIMATE and says it is 1.45× the CGC 10 quote with no published Pristine comp.

entries.title: The shelf first, the maths after
features: The Pack Shop now paints its 532-product shelf first and loads each product's price, typical return, chase maths, Sequin odds and pack contents only when that product is selected or scrolls into view. The shelf opens in newest-set order; choosing an EV or price sort weighs the shown products on demand and says so while it works.

entries.title: The shelf checks before it repeats
features: The Pack Shop no longer reuses a shelf response just because it is less than 20 seconds old. It now reuses one only while card and sealed prices, the catalogue, today's daily-deal claims and the save itself are unchanged — so a sync, a purchase that claims a deal, a snapshot restore or a save reset appears the next time you open the Shop.

entries.title: Fresh estimates after every price move
features: Pack, sealed and General Mills mini-pack estimates now refresh whenever a card price or the catalogue changes. A sync, a simulated-market roll or a pull-table rebuild can no longer leave the Pack Shop showing an old expected value, and its cached shelf response is cleared on the same signal.

entries.title: Ring up, not rip
features: The Pack Shop till now says RING UP instead of promising a rip. The purchase has always delivered the product sealed, and it still does: after you pay, open it whenever you like from Inventory → Sealed.

entries.title: Faster shelves, faster badges
features: The Achievements screen now computes set completion in one catalogue pass instead of re-scanning every card for every set. The badge wall's progress checks share that pass and the held-card valuation, so it opens in a fraction of the time and no longer blocks the rest of the dashboard.

The Pack Shop's first load now reads every pack card's TCGplayer price in one batch, then reuses each card's value across the pack estimate, sealed estimate and shelf price. The first build is several times faster, and the shelf response is reused briefly so returning to the Shop is immediate.

entries.title: Sold, asking, estimated
features: BGS 10 Black Label prices no longer treat every source as a sold quote. PriceCharting can publish a BGS 10 Black value without any Black Label sales, so the reveal and certifier label that number a PriceCharting estimate. An exact eBay Black Label comp is labelled ASKING because it comes from active listings, not completed sales. Only a sale-backed quote is labelled sold.

The activity feed and the slab certifier now use the same three labels. The BGS 10 × 1.6 fallback is explicitly a game estimate, and the grade ladder shows each rung's source and basis, so a thin or asking-price comp is visible instead of looking like a completed sale.

entries.title: Black labels, real quotes
features: BGS 10 Black Label slabs now read PriceCharting's BGS 10 Black column. When that column has a value for the exact grade, the reveal and activity feed use it instead of a 1.6× multiplier; PriceCharting can publish it without a Black Label sale, so it is not treated as a sold quote.

If PriceCharting has no Black Label price, the game checks exact-title eBay Black Label listings, which are active asking prices rather than completed sales. Ordinary BGS 10 comps no longer include Black Label listings. The estimated fallback only appears when neither external value exists.

entries.title: A premium, not a quote
features: A BGS 10 Black Label reveal and its activity line now mark a derived value ESTIMATED. When the figure is 1.6× the BGS 10 quote, the game no longer presents that derived number as a live quote even when the BGS 10 base is live.
The slab certifier still falls back to the published BGS 10 comp and says when it is doing so.

entries.title: Black labels, sealed boxes
features: Beckett Grading (BGS) is now a fourth grading service. It costs $60 a card, accepts raw cards worth $50 or more, and returns a BGS slab in 2–4 game-days. It is the only route to a BGS 10 Black Label: a 10 with four perfect subgrades, far rarer than a gem mint and valued above a BGS 10.

The Pack Shop no longer has a buy-and-rip shortcut. Every purchase now lands sealed in Inventory → Sealed, and opening it is a separate choice you make there. The Pack Opening buy list buys sealed too, instead of ripping the product immediately.
The sealed desk itself is unchanged: fresh and worn condition, selling, re-wrapping and the loan desk all still work as before.

entries.title: The handoff holds
features: The in-place updater now hands the installer to a one-time Windows scheduled task instead of a child of the closing game. The helper survives the window shutting down and runs the setup reliably.
The helper script and its log now live in TCG Life's own app-data folder, so a shell with a non-Windows TEMP path can no longer break the handoff.
This is a maintenance build for the update path; no gameplay, card data or economy rules changed.

entries.title: The loop closes
features: This is a maintenance build for the in-place updater: it verifies that a newer setup downloaded to Downloads can replace an installed copy, leave the save untouched, reopen the game automatically and land on What's New.
No gameplay, card data or economy rules changed in this build.

entries.title: Updates that install themselves
features: Installed copies now look for a newer TCG Life setup file in Downloads, Desktop and OneDrive Desktop when the game opens. No rerunning the installer by hand.

When a newer setup is found, the game shows its version and an Update now button. The game closes, runs the setup silently in place, and opens again automatically; your save, collection and settings are untouched.
The first launch after an update opens What's New by itself, so the changes in that version are the first thing you see.
If the update cannot be installed, the game reopens the version you already have instead of leaving you with no game.

entries.title: Both paces
features: Pack reveals now have a Manual reveal / Auto reveal switch beside the speed controls. Manual, the default, waits after each card for a swipe or click; Auto schedules the next card after the usual beat.
The choice carries across the packs in a session, so a whole box can be read by hand or run hands-off. Skip animation and Reveal all still work in either mode.

entries.title: At your own pace
features: Cards no longer advance on a timer. Once a card lands, it waits for a sideways swipe (or a click) before the next card comes out, so a pack is read at the player's pace instead of presenting the whole stack.

The card flip itself still runs automatically, and Skip animation and Reveal all still work when you want them. Swipe anywhere on the reveal stage; the hint under the card tells you when the next one is waiting.

entries.title: The best wrapper
features: A box rip's summary header now carries a BEST PACK total: the highest market value of any single wrapper opened so far, beside box hits and average per hit.
It updates with each pack and after a skip to the end, and it measures one wrapper's total rather than the whole box.

entries.title: The best of the box
features: A box rip's summary header now names its best hit: the highest-value card marked HIT across the wrappers opened so far, with its set and market value.
The line follows the box as it continues, so a later chase can take it. A box with no hits simply leaves the line out.

entries.title: What a hit is worth
features: A box rip's summary now shows AVG PER HIT: the mean market value of every card marked HIT across the wrappers opened so far. A big chase raises the number; bulk cards do not dilute it because only hit cards are counted.
The tile updates with each pack and after a skip to the end. A box with no hits shows a dash rather than dividing by zero.

entries.title: The box score
features: A box rip's summary now carries a BOX HITS total beside cards pulled and value. It counts every card marked HIT across every wrapper opened so far in the box, not just the pack whose page is on screen.
The count stays visible at 0 on a quiet box and updates as the box continues, including after a skip to the end.

entries.title: The whole page at once
features: The combined box summary now has Expand all and Collapse all controls for the packs on the current page. Expand all opens every wrapper together so their card grids and hit counts can be compared without opening each one by one; Collapse all folds the page back to its pack tags.
Each page keeps its own state, and the controls only act on the page in front of you. Individual pack tags still toggle, and returning to a page restores whatever was open there.

entries.title: The page remembers
features: The box summary now remembers which wrapper you had expanded on each page. Paging forward and back returns to that pack instead of collapsing the page back to its first wrapper.
The memory clears when a new rip or skip begins, so a fresh summary still opens at its first pack.

entries.title: Every wrapper's score
features: The collapsed PACK tag in a box rip now carries that wrapper's hit count beside its card count and total value. A quiet pack reads 0 hits, so the summary does not make every wrapper look the same.
The count uses the same HIT flag as the cards in the expanded sleeve, so a pack tagged 2 hits holds exactly the two cards marked HIT beneath it.

entries.title: The scorecard at the counter
features: Earlier at the counter now carries a compact tally in its header: how many offers this save claimed and how many it missed. With three past days on screen that is the last nine offers; a newer save with less history only counts the days it actually has.
The tally uses the same CLAIMED and MISSED flags as the offer rows, so the summary cannot disagree with the history beneath it.

entries.title: The other half of the shelf
features: Booster bundles and 36-pack displays now quote their own TCGplayer listing instead of being priced only from the packs inside. Sixty-six rows gained a quote — twenty-six bundles and forty displays — including Paldea Evolved at $123.74 for the bundle and $464.86 for the display, Team Up at $12,389.94, Sword & Shield at $692.76 and Primal Clash at $4,066.66.

Each number is the market for that exact listing, read through the mirror on 13 November 2026, and the shelf and till name TCGplayer rather than a model. A six-pack bundle, a 36-pack display and a half display never share a quote: only the product with a published listing gets one.

The shop now quotes 78 of its 145 bundle and display rows. The remaining 67 are older displays whose TCGplayer listings publish no market at all; they stay modelled from their packs and labelled MODEL rather than borrowing a price to fill the gap.

entries.title: The last unpriced boxes
features: Six early Elite Trainer Boxes now carry a PriceCharting sold-price value: Plasma Storm $16,225.09, Plasma Blast $7,193.29, Furious Fists $4,750.00, Phantom Forces $5,873.07, Ancient Origins $3,751.45 and Fates Collide $1,149.24.
The two XY base-set arts are priced separately rather than sharing one quote: Xerneas $4,320.61 and Yveltal $4,558.22.

Every one of these is labelled PriceCharting and dated 13 November 2026 in the shop and product note. None is presented as a TCGplayer market, and the old pack-content model is no longer used for these boxes.

entries.title: Where the price came from
features: Every sealed product on the Pack Shop shelves now carries a small QUOTE or MODEL tag. QUOTE means the price came from a published market listing — TCGplayer, PriceCharting or PokeInvest — while MODEL means it is estimated from the packs inside.
The till names the source for the selected product, and the shop header explains the two tags. Hovering a tag gives the same explanation, and daily discounts do not change the label.

entries.title: One pack at a time
features: The combined box summary now folds each pack into its own collapsible shelf tag. The tag keeps the pack number, card count and pack value visible; clicking it opens that pack and folds the one before it, so a long box can be scanned wrapper by wrapper.

The first pack on each summary page opens by default. Paging still keeps a pack whole rather than cutting its cards between pages, and a single pack or a summary without per-wrapper groups keeps its existing flat layout.

entries.title: The deals you missed
features: The Pack Shop now keeps a short record of the previous three game days' Daily Deals. Under today's board, each past day lists its three products with the discount and deal price, and marks each one CLAIMED or MISSED for this save.

The record is stored with the save, so it survives a restart. Each day's products, names and prices are snapshotted when the board is built, so a later catalogue or price change cannot rewrite what was on offer.
This is a new ledger, not a reconstruction: it begins with the first board the game records after this update. Daily Deals from before the update are not invented or backfilled.

entries.title: One deal a day
features: Each Daily Deal can now be bought only once per game day on a save. The claim is stored in the save beside the deal's day key and product, so restarting does not reset it, and the server refuses a second purchase even when the request is sent by hand.

The claim and the charge happen together: if the deal is already taken, no cash moves and no stock is added. Once claimed, that product stays off the till until the next game-day boundary, so the limit cannot be sidestepped at full price.

A deal purchase is one unit. The 10-pack lot option is removed for a booster on the board, and the board, shelf tag, till and Pack Opening's buy list mark it CLAIMED TODAY after the purchase instead of offering it again. Products not on today's board are unchanged.

entries.title: Elite boxes at their real prices
features: Elite Trainer Boxes no longer share a $32 model floor. Thirty-three standard boxes now carry the TCGplayer market for that exact listing, read from the mirror's 12 November update, including Paldea Evolved at $202.05, Silver Tempest at $155.92, Lost Origin at $193.31, Fusion Strike at $332.39 and 151 at $492.26.

The quote comes from the same TCGplayer listing as the box photo and is shown with the TCGplayer price source instead of an estimate. Pokémon Center exclusive boxes already carried their own quotes and are unchanged.

Eight older boxes — Plasma Storm, Plasma Blast and the six XY Elite Trainer Boxes — have no published TCGplayer market, so they still use the modelled price rather than borrowing another box's quote. Card prices are unchanged.

entries.title: Every wrapper from the right set
features: Multi-set Ultra-Premium Collections now open the packs they actually hold, set by set, instead of filling every wrapper from the product's anchor expansion.

The Zacian & Zamazenta box opens four each of Sword & Shield, Rebel Clash, Darkness Ablaze and Vivid Voltage; Charizard opens three each of Evolving Skies, Fusion Strike, Astral Radiance and Brilliant Stars, two Lost Origin, one Vivid Voltage and one Darkness Ablaze; Greninja opens four Paldea Evolved, two Paradox Rift, two Temporal Forces, four Twilight Masquerade and four Stellar Crown.

Mega Charizard X opens four each of Phantasmal Flames, Mega Evolution, Destined Rivals and Journey Together plus two Surging Sparks, and Moltres opens two each of Destined Rivals, Journey Together, Temporal Forces, Paradox Rift and Scarlet & Violet base plus four each of Obsidian Flames and Paldea Evolved.
Each listing's note and product manifest now state the real composition, and the notes mark the splits that come from observed openings rather than official product copy.

entries.title: Straight past the promo
features: The promo screen on a box now has a Skip to end button. It opens every remaining wrapper in one request and takes you straight to the combined summary, so a box with a promo can be ripped without watching pack 1 first.
The promo cards are still banked in your binder, and the first pack's cards are included in the summary even though they never appeared on stage.
The summary's best-pack and best-pull comparisons still use the record before the box, not the pack you skipped past.

entries.title: The box summary, wrapper by wrapper
features: Skipping to the end of a box now keeps the combined summary grouped by wrapper. Each pack gets a small PACK n label with its card count, so a 36-pack display reads as 36 pulls instead of one wall of cards.
Packs opened one at a time before the skip keep their own groups too, and paging moves whole packs to the next page rather than cutting a wrapper in half.
A single pack's summary is unchanged; it still shows the ordinary flat page.

entries.title: Three deals before the day rolls
features: The Pack Shop now has a Daily Deals board above the shelves: one booster, one box and one collection, each 10–30% off until the game-day clock rolls over. The board shows the old price, the deal price and the time left, and the shelf carries a matching discount tag.

The discount is real at the till. The board, the shelf label and the amount taken from the drawer all use the same server price; bags, single rips and the 10-pack lot are charged the deal price too. A daily deal cannot be shown without being charged.

The three picks are fixed for the game day, so restarting the game does not reroll them. On a day where a shelf lane has no product, the board fills from the other products rather than showing fewer than three deals.

entries.title: Every Ultra-Premium box on the shelf
features: The Pack Shop now carries the seven missing Ultra-Premium Collections: Sword & Shield—Zacian & Zamazenta, Sword & Shield—Charizard, Arceus VSTAR, Greninja ex, Terapagos ex, Mega Charizard X ex and Team Rocket's Moltres ex. Together with 151, Celebrations and the two 30th Celebration boxes, every UPC from 2020 through 2026 is now listed.

Each row uses the real pack count, release date, TCGplayer listing and market quote. The paper promos the catalogue actually holds are handed over: gold Zacian V and Zamazenta V, the three etched Charizard promos, Greninja ex, the three Terapagos-era gold promos, and Mega Charizard X ex with Oricorio ex. Metal-only cards and stamped variants are described rather than replaced with a different printing.

The boxes whose packs span several sets (Charizard, Greninja, Terapagos, Mega Charizard X and Moltres) open their packs from the set their listing belongs to, and the product note states that; their pack totals and prices are unchanged.

entries.title: The buttons hold still
features: The card value and hit banner now fade into a reserved slot under the card. Skip animation and Reveal all stay in the same place from the moment a pack opens, so a price appearing after the flip cannot move the controls out from under the pointer.
This applies to ordinary pulls and to massive, huge and 1st Edition banners, which share the same fixed slot.

entries.title: Skip to the last wrapper
features: Bundle, Elite Trainer Box and display summaries now have a Skip to end button. It opens every wrapper left in the box in one go and replaces the pack-by-pack pages with one binder holding every card pulled from the box.

The combined page keeps the box's total cards, value and spend, the best single pack, the new-to-binder count and the 40-card paging used by an ordinary rip. The button appears on the summary whenever the box still has wrappers.
The skip is one server request rather than a burst of 35, so a 36-pack display finishes without a long chain of requests.
A box resumed after a reload only knows the pack it resumes on; the combined page starts there and adds the rest. A box opened in one sitting includes every pack from the first wrapper onward.

entries.title: The server picks its own door
features: The desktop app no longer uses port 8787 at all. The game server asks Windows for a free port, then prints that port in its startup line; the window reads that line and loads only that address. A development server or any other program on 8787 cannot be mistaken for the game.

This closes the race left by 0.77.27 and 0.77.28. Their check could pass just before another program took 8787, and Windows could even report a port as free while a wildcard listener owned it; the game server then failed to bind and the window loaded the other program's 404.
The launch log records the port the server actually bound. If the server exits without announcing one, the splash reports a startup failure instead of opening somebody else's page.

entries.title: The port check sees the whole machine
features: The desktop app now tests port 8787 on every network interface, not only 127.0.0.1. A development server listening on 0.0.0.0 could pass the loopback-only test, so the window still loaded that server’s 404.
When 8787 is genuinely free it is still used. Otherwise the game picks a free port and gives it to its own server, which is the port the window loads.
This completes the 0.77.27 fix: the launch log records the fallback port whenever 8787 is unavailable, including when another program owns the wildcard address.

entries.title: The game opens on its own port
features: Opening the desktop app no longer shows a 404 when another program is already using port 8787. The window now chooses a free local port, gives that port to the game server, and waits for that server before loading the game.

Port 8787 is still preferred when it is available. If a development server or a leftover listener owns it, the packaged app uses the next free port instead of mistaking that listener for its own server and loading its page.
The launch log records the port the window chose, and a second copy of the app is still stopped by the single-instance guard.

entries.title: Only what was printed
features: The sealed catalogue no longer lists products that never existed. 182 phantom rows are deleted: every Booster Bundle before Lost Origin, Elite Trainer Boxes before the line began with Plasma Storm (and the expansions it skipped, like Flashfire), displays and bundles on special sets that never shipped one, and the invented wrappers around sets that only came inside another product.

That includes the subset-only sets (Shiny Vault, the Trainer Galleries, the Classic Collection, basic energy), the deck and promo sets (Southern Islands, the Trainer Kits, Detective Pikachu, Kalos Starter Set, McDonald’s 2011–19, Futsal, Pokémon Rumble) and the special-set displays for 151, Celebrations, 30th Celebration, Champion’s Path, Shining Fates, Shining Legends, Dragon Majesty and Hidden Fates. Those rows are deleted, not hidden, and the catalogue refuses to generate them again — the shop now lists only products it can stock; the three booster ids kept as pull-table hosts for the real Double Crisis, Dragon Vault and Generations boxes are never offered.

A save that already owns one of these boxes keeps that row so the stock still resolves; it stays out of the shop until it is opened or sold. Nothing is granted or refunded, and a fake marketplace listing for a Shiny Vault ETB went with the row.

The rule is sourced: the Booster Bundle line starts with Lost Origin in 2022, the Elite Trainer Box line with Plasma Storm in 2013, and a special set was sold through ETBs, tins and collections rather than a 36-pack display. Packs and displays that really shipped, including the Crown Zenith bundle and the Dragon Vault and Double Crisis blisters, are untouched.

One limitation is deliberate: `dc1-booster`, `dv1-booster` and `g1-booster` stay in the database as unsold pull-table hosts, because the real Double Crisis and Dragon Vault blisters and the Generations ETB read that table to open packs. Deleting those three rows would break three real products, so they stay behind the scenes and out of the shop.

entries.title: The rest of the collections
features: The Pack Shop now carries 31 collection products from the five special sets whose lineups it never modelled: 151, Paldean Fates, Shrouded Fable, Prismatic Evolutions and Celebrations. That includes the 151 Poster, Binder and Ultra-Premium Collections and both ex boxes, Paldean Fates’ three Tech Sticker and three Pokémon ex Premium Collections, all three Shrouded Fable illustration collections, the Prismatic Evolutions Binder, Poster, Tech Sticker, Surprise Box, Accessory Pouch, Super-Premium and Premium Figure Collections, and Celebrations’ Dragapult Prime, Deluxe Pin, V Memories, Pikachu V-UNION, Premium Figure and Ultra-Premium Collections.

Each row carries its researched contents rather than a template guess: 151’s Poster Collection is three packs plus the Bulbasaur, Charmander and Squirtle promos, the 151 Ultra-Premium Collection is sixteen packs with Mew ex and Mewtwo, and the Celebrations Ultra-Premium Collection is seventeen Celebrations packs plus eight Sword & Shield packs, the metal Pikachu and Charizard cards and the gold Pikachu V and Poké Ball.

Prices are TCGplayer market quotes for the exact product on 9 November 2026, so the 151 Ultra-Premium Collection is $843.07, the Celebrations Ultra-Premium Collection $1,206.87 and the Shrouded Fable Greninja ex collection $207.73. Every row is a real listing with its own photo, not a modelled shelf price.

Where a promo is not in this catalogue, the row names it but does not hand over a substitute: 151’s Kadabra, Abra, Electabuzz, Venusaur ex and Blastoise ex, the Shrouded Fable pre-evolutions, Prismatic Evolutions’ Espeon ex and Umbreon ex and the Surprise Box’s nine-card pool, and Celebrations’ Dragapult Prime, Pikachu V-UNION pieces and metal cards. Extra packs bundled alongside a special-set box, and accessories such as binders, posters, pins and figures, are described but not modelled.

entries.title: Every box the league had
features: The Pack Shop now sells the Build & Battle Box for every expansion that shipped one: 43 boxes from Fates Collide (2016) through Delta Reign, four packs and one of four prerelease promos in each. These were the prerelease product a league ran on, and the catalogue had no row for any of them.

The promos are real catalogue cards, not placeholders: Team Up holds Charizard, Zapdos, Nidoqueen or Jirachi; Evolving Skies holds the three Galarian birds or Flaaffy; Lost Thunder holds Suicune, Raikou, Giratina or Tapu Lele. Open a box and one of its four is dealt alongside the packs, and the shelf tag names all four.

Prices are the TCGplayer market where TCGplayer lists the box — Evolving Skies at $329.50, Lost Thunder at $204.94, Sword & Shield at $118.64 on 9 November 2026 — and 28 of the 43 carry such a quote. The other 15 are modelled at the $19.99 MSRP plus their promo, because no listing exists to quote; nothing is presented as a marketplace price that is not one.

Two honest limits. The 40-card evolution deck inside each box is not modelled, so opening one deals the four packs and the promo. And the 13 boxes TCGplayer does not carry have no box photo, so they show the set symbol rather than a picture of a product nobody photographed here.

entries.title: Only what really shipped
features: The Pack Shop has stopped offering sealed products that were never made. The Celebrations and Pokémon GO booster displays, both booster bundles, and the McDonald’s 2021 and 2022 bundles, displays and Elite Trainer Boxes were all generated by the era template rather than printed, so they are off the shelf.

Three more phantom boxes are gone with them: the Flashfire Elite Trainer Box, which the early ETB line skipped the way it skipped Plasma Freeze and Legendary Treasures, and the Call of Legends Elite Trainer Box and Booster Bundle, both of which predate the products entirely. Detective Pikachu’s bundle, display and ETB rows went too — that set only ever shipped Case Files and a Collector Chest.
Any copy you already own stays in your inventory and still opens; only the shop, pack battles and live shows stop selling them.

One deliberate exception: single packs for special sets such as Celebrations and Crown Zenith stay on the shelf even though those packs only ever came inside collections, because the card pool needs a wrapper the game can open. What is gone is the boxes those packs never came in.

entries.title: Every product gets its face
features: The Pack Shop now shows the real wrapper or box photo for every sealed product that has one. Both 30th Celebration UPCs, the 30th collection, tin and box lineup, the Delta Reign, Chaos Rising and Ascended Heroes blisters and boxes, the full Scarlet & Violet blister run, and the Double Crisis and Dragon Vault blisters were showing a set logo before because their product IDs were never wired into the art map.

Five older products whose TCGplayer listing has no usable photo — the Plasma Storm and Plasma Blast Elite Trainer Boxes, and the Aquapolis, Skyridge and Neo Discovery displays — now use a stored product photo instead of the set logo.
The McDonald's Collection 2022 pack now wears its TCGplayer wrapper photo instead of the set logo; it is listed there as the Match & Battle Pack.

The set logo is now only the fallback where no product photo exists: the catalogue rows whose wrapper never shipped and the Surging Sparks and Astral Radiance half displays, which TCGplayer lists without an image. No set logo is standing in for a photo that exists.

entries.title: Every promo on the tag
features: The Pack Shop shelf now names the promo on every product that has one, instead of only Elite Trainer Boxes and special collections. That puts the Journey Together Enhanced Booster Display's N's Reshiram topper on its shelf tag.

Selecting a product now lists its promos in the till too. A single-promo box names the card, a two-name blister lists both with a note that one is sealed inside, and a box that holds both lists both as included.

entries.title: The till scrolls itself
features: The Pack Shop till now scrolls its own contents when a product's description, pack slots or chase line get tall. Before, the panel stuck to the top while its lower half sat below the window, so scrolling moved the shelves behind it and the Ring Up & Rip button stayed out of reach.

entries.title: Back to the shelf
features: The OPEN MORE button on the pack-opening summary now takes you back to the Pack Shop shelf, with its filters and product details, instead of dropping you into Pack Opening's separate buy list.

entries.title: Pickers price in one pass
features: The screens that pick cards from your collection — Auctions, BidBay, Forum trades and local listings — were still looking up each card's TCGplayer price with a separate database query, once per row. They now load the whole batch in one query and resolve every row from it.
On a 484-card save the light inventory call now answers in about 0.075s instead of 0.138s, with the same picker fields and the same values. All 484 rows still match the full inventory endpoint.

A card without a TCGplayer price still follows the old fallback path — PriceCharting/eBay, Cardmarket, simulated or model estimate — so the shortcut never changes a quote. The full Inventory screen is untouched.

entries.title: The side doors carry less
features: The What’s New badge was downloading the entire 327KB changelog on every game boot just to compare version numbers. It now asks a 2KB summary of versions; opening the panel still loads the full entries and feature text.

Screens that only pick or list cards no longer ship fields they never draw. Pull History drops the unused image, session and printing fields (134KB → 57KB on 400 pulls), the Stream setup list keeps only the product name and price (153KB → 48KB across 464 products), and the shop’s stock, dollar-bin and grab-bag pickers drop card art and internal ids (53KB → 28KB, 81KB → 42KB and 111KB → 58KB).

The pawn counter was pricing every card twice and looking up each name separately. One price lookup and one joined name now produce the same quotes and tickets in about 0.18s instead of 0.27s on a 484-card save.
The full Shop shelf, Inventory and What’s New panel are unchanged, because those screens do use the larger rows.

entries.title: Pickers travel light
features: The screens where you choose a card — consigning to Auctions, building a BidBay lot, offering a trade on the Forum and picking cards for a local listing — were downloading the whole priced collection, including grading advice, copy drift and desk reads none of them display. They now ask a lighter endpoint for just the picker fields, while the Inventory screen keeps the full one.
