On a 484-card save that cuts the response from about 562KB to about 140KB and answers in roughly 0.14s instead of 0.26s. Every shared field — name, condition, variant, quantity, graded grade, favourite, cost and value — matched the full endpoint row for row.

The numbers a picker quotes do not change: the light rows reuse the same sellable value and the same hidden counterfeit and authentication state, so a BidBay max bid or a local listing ask comes out the same as before.

entries.title: The collection opens faster
features: Opening the collection was resolving the same card's price three times per row — the market band, this copy's drift, and the sellable value — and then asking the grading model for the same graded prices once per service. Each card's band is now resolved once and reused, the raw anchor is shared across services, and graded quotes are memoised for ten seconds.

On a 484-card save the inventory endpoint now answers in about 0.23–0.30s instead of 0.78–0.83s, and the header's state poll is around 0.11–0.15s instead of 0.16–0.31s. A full-row check against the old paths matched every value and copy price.
This is server-side only: no screen, price or button changed, and the same faster total feeds Home and the header.

entries.title: You can watch the sync run
features: Settings now draws a progress bar under Check for new sets now and Restart full sync while either job runs. A full sync shows the sets finished out of the total, then switches to a moving bar with the set it is pulling and how many cards have arrived.
A catalog check has no set count to divide, so its bar sweeps instead of inventing a percentage. Both buttons lock while a job is running and the bar clears when it finishes.

entries.title: The sample catalogue boots again
features: The bundled sample catalogue (data/catalog-seed.db) could fail at boot once it contained the 30th Celebration Mew rares. The boot repair relabelled those three cards and then rebuilt the set's pull table before the set's pack products existed, so SQLite refused the pull rows' foreign key. Products are now built for every set with cards before the rarity repairs run, and the sample save starts with its packs intact.
Existing saves were unaffected because their pack products already existed, and an empty folder still boots the way 0.77.9 made it.
Nothing on a playing save changes: this only makes the shipped sample catalogue a usable starting point again.

entries.title: Every open door sells
features: The "Which door pays most?" panel on an owned card is now four working buttons. Market listing lists the copy at market, Buylist counter sells to whichever shop currently bids highest, and once their gates open the Instant dealer and Pawn counter pay exactly what their rows quote. Each row says List or Sell and returns a receipt naming the amount.

The server re-checks the gate on every click, so the locked Resale Desk and Pawn Shop refuse a sale even if the request is hand-rolled. The buylist re-quotes before paying and refuses a stale sheet rather than quietly paying a different number.
A sale from the panel refreshes the collection and closes the card sheet; a refused door leaves the card alone and says why.

entries.title: The comparison counts only open doors
features: The "Which door pays most?" panel on an owned card was comparing four sale routes as if all four were open. A young save can only use the Market listing and the Buylist counter — the Instant dealer needs the Resale Desk ($400 cash) and the Pawn counter needs 3 sales — but both were listed as ordinary options and either could be named the best door. Locked doors are now dimmed, print what opens them, and cannot win the pick.
The footer says "Best open door" and how many doors are still locked, so the number it recommends is one you can actually walk through today.

The rest of the always-open screens were checked for the same habit. Home's shop panel, Card Shows' booth, Inventory's slab options and the other conditional panels already hide themselves until their subject exists, and Grading, Buylist and Stream name their requirements rather than assuming them, so no other copy changed.

entries.title: No lock hides its own answer
features: Stream could never open on a new save. The row asked for 5 followers, but followers are only awarded when a stream ends — so the one screen that grows your channel was the one your channel count kept shut. Stream now opens from the start; the channel's default following is what you build on.

The Card Shop's locked row now carries the terms its page used to keep to itself: $6 a day rent while cases are stocked, and that a stocked case is what turns walk-ins into sales. It still asks for $500 and names the $250 lease.

The Resale Desk's locked row now says what the desk is for: sellers leave lots priced under market, and you buy them to flip the cards. The $400 float is still the goal, but the reason to want it is visible before the door opens.

Every other gate was checked for the same problem. Deals already opens its own page and explains what counts as a sale, and the venue tabs inside print their own sales gates — nothing else was explaining the lock only after it opened.

entries.title: An empty folder still boots
features: The game no longer refuses to start when its data folder has no starter catalogue. A bare save stopped at boot on a database error from the local release products: the 30th Celebration wave ships products for a set that only exists once the catalogue has loaded, so the insert pointed at a set the save did not have. Those products now wait for a later launch instead of blocking the boot, and the save opens with the sets and cards it can insert.

A data folder is allowed to hold only data. The boot used to read schema.sql from the folder itself even when TCGLIFE_HOME pointed at a fresh or copied save directory; it now falls back to the schema that ships beside the program, so the first launch can create its database instead of failing on a missing file.

Honest note: a no-seed launch is not the same as a seeded one. It starts with the local releases (Delta Reign and the 30th Celebration promos) and fills the rest from pokemontcg.io at the normal sync pace, so the shelf is not stocked instantly the way the bundled catalogue makes it.

entries.title: The empty bench explains itself
features: Grading now explains a page that used to be blank. A save holding ten fresh pulls showed no "Worth grading now" list at all, because the panel was hidden whenever nothing cleared the bar, and the empty lab underneath told you to "Submit a card above" when there was no above. The page now names the cheapest open service, its fee and the raw value it demands, and says plainly that cheaper cards should go to the Buylist rather than pay a fee that eats the spread.
The lab's empty queue no longer points at a list that isn't there. It says a card has to clear the fee before it appears as a candidate, then waits the same game-days for its verdict.

The locked Card Shop row now reads "Save $500 · lease $250", so the number on the locked row matches the $250 hole-in-the-wall deposit on the page it opens instead of looking like a $500 minimum lease.

entries.title: The locked door explains itself
features: Clicking the locked Deals row no longer bounces you home with a one-line toast. It opens the Deals page itself: all seven venues listed, the next one marked, and the sentence that says what counts as a sale — the Market, the Buylist, the Trading Post and your shop cases. Before this, that sentence lived only on the page the lock kept you off, so the one place that answered "how do I get in?" was the one place you could not reach.

The other locked rows still stay shut, because their requirements are cash or follower counts you can already read on the row itself; only Deals carries an explanation worth opening before the gate. A deep link to a still-locked Deals venue lands on the same page with the same sentence, so "Make 3 sales" and "where do I sell?" are answered in one click.

entries.title: The first ten minutes
features: A brand-new save now opens on a short, tickable route into the game: rip a pack, sell the ones you don't keep at the Buylist, and make three sales to open the Deals district. The checklist sits on Home until the third sale and links straight to the counter that finishes each step. Before this, the only sign Deals existed was a locked sidebar row reading "Make 3 sales", and the one sentence explaining where sales come from was behind that lock.

The welcome tour now counts its six stops correctly — it said five — names the Buylist in its last step, and says welcome in rather than "Tutorial skipped" when you press Let's go. Skipping still says skipped, and Settings can still replay the tour.

The Pack Shop now defines its own shorthand. TYP is the median value of the cards inside as a share of the pack price, so TYP 80% means a typical rip returns about 80% of what you paid. The figure sits on every shelf label and was explained nowhere.

Home's activity feed no longer says "everything you did": it also carries the town's auction and resale chatter, so a four-card save was crediting the player with NPC hammers and catalogue maintenance. It now reads as what is happening in the hobby, with the player's own moves included.

entries.title: Screens on demand
features: The app shell no longer ships the whole game before the first screen paints. Each screen — Market, Card Shop, Deals, the convention floor, your binders — is now fetched the first time you open it instead of riding along in the initial download. The shell's own JavaScript fell from 1.2 MB to under 50 kB, so the sidebar and day clock appear while a screen is still arriving, and screens you have already visited open from cache.

This is a loading change, not a rendering one: the first screen still needs the shared card and foil renderer, so what you notice is the faster shell and quicker returns to screens you have already opened, not a lighter card grid. The dev-only holofoil inspector is no longer included in a packaged build at all.

entries.title: Every screen says what happened
features: A failed first load no longer spins forever or invents an empty shelf. The collection offered to sell you your first pack over a catalogue that never answered, the binder shelf invited you to make a first binder while yours still existed, the resale desk claimed no notes were on the counter, pull history said you had never opened a pack, the ship bay showed a clean queue, and a card sheet stayed on "Loading card…" indefinitely. They now name what did not load, stay put on a failed background refresh, and retry on request.

A failed fetch no longer reads as a real zero. Home said you had no record, no digest and no activity; the Community board said zero threads; the Trading Post said no traders in town; the Marketplace showed six zeroes and "no quotes"; the stream room offered to go live with no products; and your inventory showed an empty binder. Each screen now says what it could not load and offers Try again, and keeps the last good data when a background poll fails rather than blanking the page.

Panels that used to disappear are now honest about it. Your storage box returned nothing at all until its fetch answered; the shop's tax desk, books, staff roster and accountant vanished the same way; and the convention floor simply showed no floor when its call failed. They now say they are reading, or that the read failed, and retrying actually retries. Settings no longer prints "Cards 0" and "Sets synced —" while it is still reading the database, and the notification bell distinguishes "nothing yet" from "the server did not answer".

entries.title: The whole card, no scrolling
features: Pack Opening's reveal card is now sized by the height of your window as well as its width. It used to take 400px of width whatever the window did — and 60% of the window's width once the window was narrower than that — so on a short screen the card on its own stood taller than the page could show: at 1000x650 it drew an 837px card under its value, progress dots and buttons, and the bottom of every pull sat below the fold. You had to scroll mid-reveal to see the card you had just turned over.

Above roughly 1030px of window height nothing changes — the card is still 400px wide. Below that it shrinks just enough for the card, its value, the dots and the Skip animation / Reveal all buttons to fit in one view: about 325px wide on a 1440x944 window, smaller than that in a short one, and the fan of cards behind it shrinks with it so the stack never looks wider than the card it is holding. The stage no longer insists on a 560px floor (600px for a sealed wrapper) taller than the window either, and the wrapper on the tear screen shrinks with the window in the same way, so the pack stage fits too. Cards you have already pulled are unaffected: the summary binder scrolls as before.

entries.title: Ten cards, not six
features: 30th Celebration collections were advertising the wrapper's six cards while every rip dealt ten. The two-pack blister said 12 cards and opened 20, and the binder, Knock Out Collection, mini tin, poster collection, Tech Sticker Collection, Sylveon ex and Greninja ex boxes had the same split. The shelf, the slot list and the opener now all say ten game cards; the manifest still records the physical six-card wrapper — five cards plus a foil Basic Energy — separately, because the game's ten-card abstraction is not a claim about the wrapper.

entries.title: Every box gets a face
features: Sealed shelf cards no longer leave an empty art slot when TCGplayer has no wrapper photo. The 79 sold products without a photo now show their set's logo, and a wrapper photo that fails to load falls back to that logo too. If the logo itself is unavailable or broken, the set symbol and finally a package mark remain behind it, so every facing has an image. The logo is only a stand-in for the missing product photo: the product's own name, price and promo badge are unchanged.

The Pack Shop header no longer stretches into a tall empty column. Its OPEN badge, title, description and cash balance now sit in the compact header row they were designed for, with the shelves beginning directly below.

entries.title: The box hands you the promo
features: Sealed shelf cards now name the promo included before you buy. Elite Trainer Boxes, blisters and collections show the card beside their art and price — the four split boxes read PROMO · Koraidon, PROMO · Miraidon, PROMO · Riolu and PROMO · Alakazam, while a poster collection or Ultra-Premium Collection prints its full promo list on the shelf tag, with the longest three-name list wrapping onto a second line. A product whose copy names one of two still says “or” rather than implying both are inside, and a product with no documented promo shows no badge.

Regular Scarlet & Violet and Mega Evolution Elite Trainer Boxes now show the art you are buying. Each shipped in two versions, and the shop treats them as separate SKUs with the promo that art pins: Koraidon → Koraidon (SVP 014), Miraidon → Miraidon (SVP 013), Mega Lucario → Riolu (MEP 010) and Mega Gardevoir → Alakazam (MEP 009). The old rows named both promos and handed over one by chance; the original ids keep Koraidon and Mega Lucario so stock already in a save stays put. TCGplayer markets read on 8 November 2026 price the four boxes at $131.73, $144.80, $114.85 and $112.42, each with its own box photo. The Pokémon Center versions already used these same art-to-promo pairs.

Primal Clash and BREAKthrough Elite Trainer Boxes now show both arts, with the box you buy carrying its own contents and its own price. Each is the real eight-pack box: 65 sleeves matching that art, 45 Energy cards, the set's player's guide, six damage-counter dice, a coin-flip die, two acrylic condition markers, a collector's box with four dividers and a TCGO code card — and no promo card, which the notes now say outright. The contents come from Pokémon.com's Primal Clash and BREAKthrough product pages. TCGplayer publishes no market price for three of the four arts, so the shop names the source it used rather than passing a secondary quote off as TCGplayer: Primal Groudon is $7,168.38 and Primal Kyogre $7,500.00 by PokeInvest on 8 November 2026, Mewtwo X is $1,598.41 by PriceCharting with a recorded $1,600.00 sale on 31 October 2026, and Mewtwo Y keeps TCGplayer's $1,499.00 market. PriceCharting's Groudon guide is lower at $5,795.75; the box follows PokeInvest's newer sealed-sale figure and names that source in its note. These are secondary-market readings, not official prices.

The Black & White shelf was rebuilt against the era's own products. Elite Trainer Boxes did not exist for every set: the line began with Plasma Storm, which held seven packs, and Plasma Blast added the eighth — the other ten BW boxes in the catalogue are gone. No Black & White expansion shipped a six-pack Booster Bundle either, so all of those rows are refused. Dragon Vault was never a normal set: its 21 cards came in five-card packs sold only inside three-pack blisters, so the standalone booster and the 36-pack display are refused and the blister is now its own openable product at three packs of five, priced at the exact blister's $1,995.90 TCGplayer market. Nine BW packs carry their own TCGplayer quotes too — $110 for Emerging Powers up to $651.13 for Plasma Storm — while Dragons Exalted and Boundaries Crossed publish no market and stay on the model, as do all eleven 36-pack displays. The blister's one-of-five Mirror Holofoil variant cards are a random accessory, not a fixed promo, so they are not handed over.

XY packs and displays now sell at what the marketplace charges for that exact wrapper or box, not at a value modelled from the cards inside. All twelve main-set booster packs carry a TCGplayer market read on 8 November 2026 — $33.65 for Steam Siege up to $229.72 for Phantom Forces — and seven of the twelve displays do too: Furious Fists $4,717.50, Roaring Skies $4,768.42, Ancient Origins $9,807.99, BREAKthrough $3,265.81, Fates Collide $2,754.99, Steam Siege $1,436.99 and Evolutions $2,707.61. The five displays whose TCGplayer listings publish no market — XY base, Flashfire, Phantom Forces, Primal Clash and BREAKpoint — deliberately stay on the model rather than borrowing another box's price. These are collector-market quotes for out-of-print sealed product, so a single XY pack now costs far more than its $3.99 sticker did.

Double Crisis can be opened again. Instead of refusing the set's invented booster, display and ETB, the shelf now carries the product that actually existed: a four-pack blister of seven-card packs. Opening it deals 28 cards across four wrappers, and it sells for $1,715.52 — four times the single pack's $428.88 TCGplayer market, because no blister quote exists, so the price is derived rather than listed. The wrapper is modelled as those four packs. While wiring the seven-card pack, special products now honour their own declared card count instead of assuming ten, which also corrects the 30th Celebration collections to their six-card packs.

The XY line's sealed shelf has been rebuilt against the era's own product copy. Every main XY Elite Trainer Box now opens eight packs instead of nine — Pokémon.com's box copy and Bulbapedia's composition table both say eight — and the boxes are split by art where two shipped: Xerneas / Yveltal, Primal Groudon / Primal Kyogre, Mewtwo X / Mewtwo Y and Mega Charizard Y / Mega Blastoise. Roaring Skies, BREAKpoint and Steam Siege ETBs now sell at their TCGplayer quotes ($7,899.99, $1,099.99 and $1,800), while the two-art boxes whose listings carry no market price stay on the modelled price and say so. Three products that never existed are gone: no XY expansion shipped a six-pack Booster Bundle, the Kalos Starter Set was three 39-card decks, and Generations packs came only inside Mythical and Red & Blue collections. Generations' one real box is corrected to ten packs with the Shaymin-EX promo, Double Crisis's invented booster, display and ETB are refused (its seven-card packs came only in four-pack blisters), and the Evolutions display stays on the shelf where it belongs.

Eight regular Elite Trainer Boxes that shipped in two arts are now two SKUs each, so the box you buy is the box you see: Sun & Moon (Solgaleo / Lunala), Ultra Prism (Dawn Wings / Dusk Mane Necrozma), Sword & Shield (Zacian / Zamazenta), Battle Styles (Single Strike / Rapid Strike Urshifu), Chilling Reign (Ice Rider / Shadow Rider Calyrex), Evolving Skies (the two Eeveelution four-packs), Paradox Rift (Iron Valiant / Roaring Moon) and Temporal Forces (Walking Wake / Iron Leaves). Each art carries its own TCGplayer quote read on 8 November 2026 — Sun & Moon is $248.05 / $246.84, Ultra Prism $780.99 / $760.77, Evolving Skies $546.57 / $456.06 — and its own box photo, instead of one row priced from the pack model. The original id keeps the first art, so existing stock stays on it. Paradox Rift and Temporal Forces also pin each art's promo (Iron Bundle with Iron Valiant, Scream Tail with Roaring Moon, Flutter Mane with Walking Wake, Iron Thorns with Iron Leaves), matching the Pokémon Center boxes.

Every Pokémon Center Elite Trainer Box now sells at its own TCGplayer quote, not at a value guessed from the packs inside it. The twenty boxes that still used the pack model were the worst-priced items on the shelf: Paldea Evolved sat at $104 while the box trades near $590, 151 at $174 against $1,152, Destined Rivals at $84 against $403, and Ascended Heroes at $133 against $323. All 38 Pokémon Center boxes — Sword & Shield through Delta Reign — now carry a marketplace number read on 8 November 2026, with the quote's listing photo used where a box had no art.

The Sword & Shield Elite Trainer Box Plus is on the shelf, in both arts: Zacian at $235.67 and Zamazenta at $240.64, the TCGplayer market for each box on 8 November 2026. These were the international half of the 2020 Ultra-Premium Collection — North America got the combined box instead — and each holds twelve packs, three each from Sword & Shield, Rebel Clash, Darkness Ablaze and Vivid Voltage, plus a gold full-art Zacian V or Zamazenta V. The metal dice, coin and condition markers are accessories and are not modelled.

That box needed something no other product did: its twelve packs come from four different expansions. The opener now follows the real composition — three packs of each set, in that order — instead of dealing twelve packs of its host set, and every way of ripping it (whole box, one wrapper at a time, pack battles and tournaments) deals the mix. The product page says so plainly rather than implying a single-set box.

The two-art Pokémon Center boxes are separate products now. Chilling Reign, Evolving Skies, Scarlet & Violet, Paradox Rift, Temporal Forces and Mega Evolution each shipped their Pokémon Center Elite Trainer Box in two arts, and the catalogue carried one row with one quote and a note naming the other version's price. Each art is its own box on the shelf, with its own photo and its own TCGplayer quote read on 8 November 2026: Chilling Reign $209.63 Ice Rider and $191.93 Shadow Rider, Evolving Skies $1,087.99 Jolteon art and $1,127.56 Glaceon art, Scarlet & Violet $286.56 Koraidon and $316.89 Miraidon, Paradox Rift $188.73 Iron Valiant and $205.75 Roaring Moon, Temporal Forces $197.48 Iron Leaves and $212.81 Walking Wake, and Mega Evolution $177.19 Mega Gardevoir and $194.26 Mega Lucario. The original row keeps the first art, so any stock already in a save stays where it was.

Each split box now carries the promo printed on its own art instead of a one-of draw between the pair. The Koraidon box seals Koraidon and the Miraidon box Miraidon; Iron Valiant seals Iron Bundle while Roaring Moon seals Scream Tail; Iron Leaves seals Iron Thorns while Walking Wake seals Flutter Mane; Mega Gardevoir seals Alakazam and Mega Lucario seals Riolu. Every one of those boxes holds the card twice, plain and with the Pokémon Center logo, and the stamp is still not modelled as a separate paper, so the box hands the card over once.

Sun & Moon Elite Trainer Boxes hold eight packs, not nine. The whole era from Sun & Moon base through Cosmic Eclipse was seeded with the later nine-pack format, so every box was opening a pack it never held. The three special sets are the exception at ten, and each now hands over the promo that was sealed inside: Shining Legends a Shining Ho-Oh, Dragon Majesty a Naganadel-GX and Hidden Fates a Moltres & Zapdos & Articuno-GX. Dragon Majesty's row opens ten packs because Bulbapedia's contents table and the published box copy both say ten; TCGplayer's own metadata says nine, and the note records the disagreement rather than hiding it.

The Sun & Moon shelf had products that never existed. No six-pack Booster Bundle shipped anywhere in the era, so the bundles listed for all twelve main sets and the three special sets are gone from sale. Shining Legends, Dragon Majesty and Hidden Fates never had a 36-pack Booster Display either, and Detective Pikachu had no Elite Trainer Box, bundle or display at all — its four-card packs only ever came inside the Case Files and collections, so its booster row now deals four cards instead of ten. The rows stay in the save so existing stock is untouched, but the shop will not sell them.

Hidden Fates' Shiny Vault is no longer sold as sealed product. The 94-card subset only ever existed inside Hidden Fates packs, and the catalogue had generated a booster, bundle, display and Elite Trainer Box for it out of the set's shape. Those four rows are now refused for sale, so the only way to a Shiny Vault card is a Hidden Fates pack, which is how the real product worked.

Sun & Moon boxes now sell at what they actually trade for. A 2017–2019 sticker is not today's price: the base set's Elite Trainer Box now lists at its $248.05 market instead of $39.99, Lost Thunder's at $729.80, Cosmic Eclipse's at $1,874.50 and Team Up's at $4,000, with every quote read from TCGplayer for the exact box on 8 November 2026. Where a box shipped in two art versions the row carries one quote and names the other version's price — Sun & Moon's Lunala box at $246.84 beside Solgaleo's $248.05, and Ultra Prism's Dusk Mane box at $760.77 beside Dawn Wings' $780.99.

Sword & Shield Elite Trainer Boxes hold eight packs, not nine. Every box from Sword & Shield base through Silver Tempest was being seeded with the nine-pack format that came later, so each was opening a pack it never held and pricing off it. Bulbapedia's contents table gives eight for the whole era, and the Silver Tempest box's own copy says eight. Champion's Path and Shining Fates are the exception at ten, and both of theirs carried a promo the catalogue was not handing over: Champion's Path a full-art Charizard V and Shining Fates an Eevee VMAX.

The Sword & Shield shelf had products that were never printed. No six-pack Booster Bundle existed before Lost Origin, so the bundles listed for Sword & Shield through Brilliant Stars are gone, along with Champion's Path's and Shining Fates' — and neither of those two special sets ever had a 36-pack Booster Display either, so those boxes are gone too. The era's real bundles are Lost Origin, Silver Tempest and Crown Zenith, and Crown Zenith's was missing from the catalogue entirely; it is on the shelf now at its $217.13 market. These rows stay in the save so existing stock is untouched, but the shop will not sell them.

The Sword & Shield boxes the catalogue never listed are here. Evolving Skies and Astral Radiance shipped European eighteen-pack half displays, priced like the Scarlet & Violet halves at half a display's sticker with the pack-value floor under them. Every Pokémon Center box from Chilling Reign to Silver Tempest is now on the shelf too — ten packs instead of eight, twelve for Crown Zenith's Plus box, and Chilling Reign's eight because of the packaging error Bulbapedia records. None of those carries a second stamped promo, which began with Scarlet & Violet, and each sells at the TCGplayer market for the exact box rather than a model: $182.26 for Astral Radiance up to $1,087.99 for Evolving Skies.

Hit rates were checked across the line: every Sword & Shield set that has cards has a pull table, so no set was being opened against an empty odds profile. The odds themselves are the era's researched profile rather than a per-set measurement, which is unchanged.

The new displays show their own boxes now. The Enhanced Journey Together display and the five half displays were drawing the set symbol because the artwork matcher only recognises a set's standard wrapper — these are separate SKUs whose photos sit on their own TCGplayer product pages. Each now wears the exact photo of that box, keyed to the same product id its price came from: the Enhanced box with its topper and four of the five eighteen-pack half boxes, none of them borrowing the standard display's picture. The fifth, the Surging Sparks half box, has no photo published anywhere — TCGplayer lists the product but answers 403 for its image at every size — so it keeps the set symbol rather than wearing the full display's picture.

The Pokémon Center Elite Trainer Boxes are on the shelf — every set that shipped one: Scarlet & Violet through Destined Rivals, 151, Paldean Fates, Shrouded Fable, Prismatic Evolutions, Black Bolt, White Flare, the Mega Evolution line from Mega Evolution through Delta Reign, Ascended Heroes and the 30th Celebration box. Each holds eleven packs instead of the regular box's nine, so it costs more and opens more: it sells at the $59.99 Pokémon Center charged, floored by what eleven packs are worth and with the promo counted on top.

Each Pokémon Center box carries the set's ETB promo twice — one plain and one with the Pokémon Center logo — and that second copy is the same card, not a second printing. The stamp is not modelled as its own paper, the same simplification the Prismatic Eevee and the Journey Together N's Reshiram already carry, so the box hands the card over once rather than inventing a duplicate card for your binder. None of these boxes has a TCGplayer quote here because they were Pokémon Center exclusives, and several now trade for four to six times what they cost; the shop prices an in-print box at its shelf price, so the Pokémon Center version sits above the regular one without pretending to be the collector market.

Journey Together now has its Enhanced Booster Display on the shelf: thirty-six packs plus a Box Topper, the illustration rare N's Reshiram 116/159 carrying a Journey Together stamp. It was a separate SKU sold through Pokémon Center and by Play! Pokémon retailers, and the ordinary display has no topper. It sells at TCGplayer's $225.73 market for the exact box, read on 8 November 2026. The stamp is not modelled as a separate paper, so the card you receive is the set's ordinary N's Reshiram — the same simplification the Prismatic Eevee already carries.

The 18-pack half displays are on the shelf: Twilight Masquerade, Stellar Crown, Surging Sparks, Journey Together and Destined Rivals. They are the half-size boxes sold in European markets — Bulbapedia records the Twilight Masquerade ones and TCGplayer lists all five as Half Booster Box, with Stellar Crown at $253.23, Surging Sparks at $193.27 and Destined Rivals at $317.50 read on 8 November 2026. The other two have no listed price here, so they sell at half a display's MSRP floored by what their packs are worth. A half display deals eighteen packs and is priced and battled as eighteen, not thirty-six.

The MEP Black Star Promos are in the catalogue: 116 printings with their real numbers, artwork and TCGplayer market prices — including the four Delta Reign Build & Battle Box promos (Masquerain, Magmortar, Enamorus and Kommo-o), which the promo set's own feed did not carry and which come from the TCGplayer mirror instead. They are the promo run behind the whole Mega Evolution line, so the boxes that seal one can finally hand over the card that was in the box.

30th Celebration boxes now give their actual promos. The Poster Collection gives Articuno, Zapdos and Moltres; the Tech Sticker Collection gives Alolan Exeggutor or Lucario; the Sylveon ex and Greninja ex boxes give their own ex; the Elite Trainer Box gives Nidorina; the Ditto Premium Collection gives Ditto; the Mew and Mewtwo figure collections give their Pokémon; and the Ultra-Premium Collections give Pikachu ex with Espeon ex by day, Pikachu ex with Umbreon ex by night.

Ascended Heroes does too. The Elite Trainer Box gives N's Zekrom; the Premium Poster Collection gives Mega Lucario ex or Mega Gardevoir ex; the three Mega ex boxes give Mega Meganium ex, Mega Emboar ex and Mega Feraligatr ex. The Tech Sticker Collection and First Partners Deluxe Pin Collection use the Ascended Heroes set cards they actually carry — Charmander 020 or Gastly 123, and Chikorita 008, Tepig 029 and Totodile 041 — on the Pixel Cosmos Holofoil those boxes print, which this build does not model as a separate paper.
The product pages now map each named promo to its printing instead of only naming it, so the promo panel in a manifest shows the card and its value.

Three 2-Pack Blisters join the shelf. The 30th Celebration one is the other product carrying the 116/128 Eevee — two packs, that foil promo and a plastic coin for $9.99 — and hands it over like the Knock Out Collection. The Prismatic Evolutions 2-Pack Blister gives the Eevee promo with the Pokémon Day 2025 stamp, a Cosmos Parallel Holofoil of the set's Eevee 074/131, plus a metallic coin for $9.99. The Ascended Heroes 2-Pack Blister gives Erika's Tangela or Larry's Komala from the set's own 007/217 and 175/217 printings, with a Gym Leader coin.

Single Pack and Three Pack Blisters are a family of their own now, for the thirteen sets whose promos the sources name card by card: Scarlet & Violet (Spidops, Espathra / Arcanine, Dondozo), Paldea Evolved (Smoliv, Growlithe / Tinkatink, Varoom), Obsidian Flames (Pawmi, Paldean Wooper / Houndstone, Eevee), Paradox Rift (Pineco, Sinistea / Cetitan, Arctibax), Temporal Forces (Carvanha, Bellibolt / Cleffa, Cyclizar), Twilight Masquerade (Toxel, Pupitar / Revavroom, Snorlax), Stellar Crown (Horsea, Porygon2 / Latias, Tinkaton), Surging Sparks (Wooper, Pachirisu / Quagsire, Zapdos), Destined Rivals (Zarude, Eevee / Zebstrika, Kangaskhan), Delta Reign (Spritzee / Seel), and Mega Evolution, Phantasmal Flames and Chaos Rising from the MEP run. A three-pack sells for the published $13.99; a single has no published MSRP, so it is priced from the pack's price with the promo counted on top, and every one of them hands over the card Bulbapedia files with that product.

Some blisters are deliberately missing. Perfect Order shipped blisters too, but their promo numbers were not sourced here, and Journey Together's sit at SVP 185 to 188, past the range mapped in this pass. They make no claim rather than a guessed one.

Where the blister evidence is thinner, the notes say so. The 30th Celebration blister was never on the official showcase, so its contents and price come from Bill's Archive's product guide; no published MSRP was found for the Ascended Heroes blister, so its price is the $12.99 retail listing Academy shows, and retailers disagree about whether it landed on 30 January or 20 February 2026. The stamped cosmos Eevee and the Trainer's Pokémon variants are held as their set cards, because this build does not model those stamps as separate papers.

The shop prices a special collection honestly now. Mini tins, poster collections and the premium boxes all shared one "special" price rule and every one of them landed on the same $90 floor; each now sells at its published shelf price, floored by what its packs are worth. A guaranteed promo also counts toward the price, so a box can no longer cost less than the card sealed inside it — the 30th Celebration Elite Trainer Box carries a $49 Nidorina, and its shelf price has to reflect that.

Delta Reign's two blisters name MEP 115 and MEP 116 for their promos, and those numbers are redirects: Bulbapedia files Spritzee and Seel as reprints of Perfect Order 35 and 18, so the boxes hand over those set cards, exactly as the Knock Out Collection's Eevee turned out to be 116/128. The Pixel Cosmos Holofoil those two blisters print is not modelled as a paper of its own, so the copy in your binder is the set card's ordinary one. The Elite Trainer Box is the same story from the other side: its Kyogre is Delta Reign's own 26/103, filed as MEP 117, so that box now hands over the set card too instead of naming a promo it could not find. Both blisters also sell at what they actually trade for on TCGplayer — $13.08 for the single and $19.05 for the three-pack — instead of the pack's price plus the promo, and no model is allowed to override a real quote: the game's own pack valuation had marked the $19.05 three-pack up to $47. The Knock Out Collection's Eevee turned out not to be a Black Star Promo at all. Bulbapedia's 30th Anniversary table lists it as 116/128 Eevee [Cosmos Holofoil] — the numbered set card, also carried by the 2-Pack Blister — so the box now hands over that card. The stamped cosmos printing is not modelled as its own paper, so the copy in your binder is the set card's ordinary one. Fourteen of the 116 MEP promos have no TCGplayer price on the source read here, so they are catalogued but never handed out; none of the boxes above depends on one. Prices, art and numbering are the source's, not measured from a physical card.

The whole Mega Evolution line now uses its own measured pack odds instead of a generic hit table. No profile ever carried a Mega Hyper Rare tier, so every gold card from Mega Evolution through Delta Reign was dealt at a 1-in-50 weight; each set now uses the count the TCGplayer Authentication Centre published for it — Mega Evolution and Phantasmal Flames 1 in 1,260, Ascended Heroes 1 in 540, Perfect Order 1 in 1,786, Chaos Rising 1 in 956, Pitch Black 1 in 1,081 and Delta Reign about 1 in 1,000. Ascended Heroes also gets its own Mega Attack Rare at 1 in 29 and the Ultra Rare rate that tier displaces (1 in 21). Delta Reign's modelled pack content falls from $15.80 to $6.32 — about the $6.35 a pack the $19.05 three-pack works out to on TCGplayer — so the ESTIMATE line and the shelf price agree instead of the valuation claiming the box was worth $47. Two older sets had measured tiers sitting on the same fallback and are pinned too: Paldean Fates prints a Shiny Ultra Rare 1 in 13 packs and a Shiny Rare 1 in 4, and Crown Zenith prints its secret rares 1 in 133 rather than 1 in 50. The odds are community counts, not official ones — The Pokémon Company publishes none — and the rarest tiers rest on few pulls (one gold Rayquaza in Delta Reign's pre-release sample), so treat 1 in 1,000 as an estimate rather than a measurement. Sets outside these eight keep the era profile; the full audit is in reports/hit-odds-audit.md.

Crown Zenith no longer puts a Galarian Gallery card in every pack. The gallery cards ride the reverse-holo position, and this build filled that position with a gallery card every single time, which valued a Crown Zenith pack at $44.28; the gallery is really in 35.2% of packs, so the other 64.8% now deal an ordinary reverse holo and a pack is worth $18.04. The booster's shelf price falls with it, from $132.90 to $18.04. The same 35.2% replaces the era's 9% figure in the gallery-only table, which is never sold but was wrong in the other direction. The odds are TCGplayer's per-rarity count rather than an official figure.

Out-of-print appreciation no longer stacks on top of a modern box's contents. Sealed was estimated as content value times the scarcity curve times the demand curve, so a $55 Crown Zenith Elite Trainer Box holding $180 of packs priced at $790. Modern sealed (2011 onwards) now prices at what its packs are worth, with the box discount applied. Crown Zenith's Elite Trainer Box falls from $790 to $146.65 and its booster from $54.15 to $14.33; Scarlet & Violet's ETB lands at $51.56 and Paldean Fates' at $114.84, both within reach of what they sell for. Pre-2011 boxes keep the collector curve, because there the sealed box is itself the asset rather than a bag of packs — Base Set's display is unchanged. The remaining gap on Crown Zenith is its own pack value: 35.2% of packs carry a Galarian Gallery card and the set's 70 gallery cards are all priced, so its ten packs still read at $155.80 of contents. That floor is the anti-money-printer rule, not a multiplier.

The sealed floor now values a box's packs at what selling the pulls actually pays. It was priced against the sticker market value of the contents, which nobody collects: the instant dealer pays 70-92%, a market listing pays market minus a 10% commission, the best buylist 75% and the pawn shop 40%. Every box was therefore floored above its own contents' realizable worth. The floor uses the best route of the four, so buying at it still cannot be turned into a profit by any route, but a box may now sit below its packs' sticker price the way real boxes do. Paldean Fates' Elite Trainer Box, whose contents are priced cleanly, falls from $123.08 to $114.84. The floor is still a floor, and it is what stops a box from being a printer: Crown Zenith's price is set entirely by what its packs hold, which is a card-value question rather than a sealed one.

The Galarian Gallery no longer hands each of its 70 cards the same chance. The gallery fills Crown Zenith's bonus slot in 35.2% of packs and the pool was split evenly, so the $290 Giratina VSTAR pulled exactly as often as a $2 Thievul. With the gallery carrying 81% of a pack's value, that flat pool priced a pack at $18.04. The four GG secrets now pull at the researched 1 in 500 packs each, which is 0.8% of packs and agrees with TCGplayer's 0.75-0.80% secret rate, and the other 66 cards share the remaining 34.4% evenly. That split inside the gallery is this build's distribution, not a measured one: only the secret tier has a per-card figure, so the rest is an even share. A Crown Zenith pack is worth $15.58, sells at $14.33, and the Elite Trainer Box lands at $146.65.

The other six bonus subsets had the same two faults: each was dealt into every single pack and each card in it had an equal share. Hidden Fates was handing out a Shiny Vault card in all 100% of packs; a Shiny Vault card really lands in 35.8% of them (21.2% baby shinies, 10.19% Shiny GX, 3.42% full-art Trainers, 1.01% gold, from Pokecompare's Elite Fourum table), so its pack value falls from $63.80 to $25.31. Shining Fates uses ThePriceDex's per-rarity rates — Shiny Rare 1 in 4.4 packs, Shiny V 1 in 19.8, Shiny VMAX 1 in 25.5, SV Secret 1 in 109.9 — for 32.6% of packs instead of all of them: $9.29 to $5.50 a pack. The four Trainer Galleries fill their slot in about one pack in eight rather than every pack, which puts a pack at $7.52 for Vivid Voltage, $6.54 for Battle Styles, $8.02 for Chilling Reign and $5.14 for Lost Origin. Lost Origin's gallery keeps its researched tier split; the other three share their slot evenly and use TCGplayer's 12.31% Lost Origin count, because no source read here publishes a per-tier table for them.

Foil was missing on 1,109 cards: the locally-seeded releases (Delta Reign, the 30th Celebration products) keep their artwork on a different image host from the rest of the catalogue, and the game's own copy of a card — the one the foil reads its pixels from — asked for a file that only exists on the old host. Those cards failed to load that copy and rendered flat, so a 30th Celebration holo showed no foil at all. The copy now falls back to whichever image the card actually uses, so every card with artwork gets its paper.

The Home dashboard claimed it was still building the card database and that 0 real cards were priced, on a save holding 20,898 priced cards. The sync's card counter only moved while a set was being fetched, so a start-up that found every set already synced reported zero — its first paint then quoted that zero as fact. The counter now reads the catalogue at boot and again when a pass ends, and the dashboard says "Reading the card catalogue…" until it has an answer instead of guessing.

Every holo card now has a shine: a slow violet-to-gold iridescent band travels across the card with one narrow white glint inside it — colour first, light second — staggered per card so a binder page glints rather than blinking in unison. Only cards whose printing actually has foil sweep — a plain common stays still — and the review link, the hover zoom, the slab well and the pack-opening reveal all show it, because they all render the same card component now. Cards no longer show a second, smaller copy of themselves sitting on top of them. The holo layer is computed at a small fixed size and then stretched over the card, and it was being drawn at that small size instead — centred on the card, so a holofoil card appeared to have a shrunken twin floating over its own artwork. It now fills the card exactly, which is where the duplicate came from on the collection grid and in the card detail view. The hover preview also sits beside a card rather than under your cursor, and is switched off inside the card detail view, where the card is already large.

A box that holds more than one promo now hands over every card inside it: the 30th Celebration Ultra-Premium Collections give Pikachu ex with Espeon ex by day or Umbreon ex by night, the Poster Collection gives all three Legendary Birds, and the Ascended Heroes First Partners Deluxe Pin Collection gives Chikorita, Tepig and Totodile. Before, each of those handed over one card from the group, chosen by a hash of the product id. Blisters and the Tech Sticker Collections are unchanged on purpose — their evidence says the box held one of two, so one is what a rip gives. The same rule fixes two prices: the promo contribution is now summed for a box that holds every named promo instead of averaged, so the day UPC counts $118.71 of promos rather than $59.36 and the night box $141.64 rather than $70.82, and each of those promos is marked guaranteed on the product rather than a one-in-three chance.

The five Mega Evolution Elite Trainer Boxes now hand over the promo that was in the box. Bulbapedia's MEP promo table files Alakazam (MEP 009) with the Mega Gardevoir box, Riolu (MEP 010) with the Mega Lucario box, Charcadet (MEP 022) with Phantasmal Flames, Tyrunt (MEP 070) with Perfect Order, Fennekin (MEP 080) with Chaos Rising and Zarude (MEP 088) with Pitch Black, so each box grants that card and its value now counts toward the shelf price. The names had been recorded since 0.75.0 without a catalogue id, so those boxes granted nothing at all. MEP 003 Alakazam is the Build & Battle Box printing and MEP 059 Fennekin is another promotion, so neither is the ETB card. The Mega Evolution box shipped in two versions, so it still hands over one of Riolu or Alakazam, which is what a real box contained.

Black Bolt's and White Flare's Elite Trainer Boxes finally hand over their promos: Thundurus (SVP 209) for Black Bolt and Tornadus (SVP 210) for White Flare. Both cards were named on the box all along but had no catalogue row — pokemontcg.io has not published 209 or 210, and its image paths return nothing — so the box granted no card and its price ignored the one inside. They are indexed as SVP promos with the plain ETB printing's TCGplayer market, Thundurus $1.50 and Tornadus $1.09, read through TCGdex on 8 November 2026; the Pokémon Center stamped copies TCGdex reports at about $17.33 and $14.41 are separate printings this build does not model, so the box hands over the ordinary card. Prices are a marketplace reading, not an official price line.

Black Bolt and White Flare no longer price off a mislabelled chase card. Their two Victini Black White Rare cards (171/086 and 172/086) came from the catalogue labelled as ordinary rares, so a $600+ card was dealt as often as a bulk rare: a pack valued at $105 and the Elite Trainer Box at $875. Both now sit in the Black White Rare pool, and the sets deal the pull rates TCGplayer measured over 700+ packs instead of the generic era ladder — a Black Bolt pack values at about $9 and its Elite Trainer Box at about $85, against a $13.74 pack on the secondary market. Black White Rare never appeared in that sample, so its 1-in-496 rate is the community estimate, not a count.

The Crown Zenith Elite Trainer Box now hands over the promo that was actually sealed inside it, Lucario VSTAR SWSH291 — the etched foil print named on the box and by Bulbapedia. It had been granting SWSH214, a different Lucario VSTAR promo worth about $2 on TCGplayer instead of about $8.50.

Prismatic Evolutions packs now deal the rates TCGplayer measured over 1,200 packs instead of the generic Scarlet & Violet ladder: a Double Rare about 1 in 6 packs, an Ultra Rare 1 in 13, an ACE SPEC 1 in 21 and a gold Hyper Rare 1 in 180, with the 32 art rares staying at the set's 1-in-45 Special Illustration Rare rate. The previous ladder was handing out a rare-or-better card in 37% of packs; the measured figure is about 29%.

entries.title: Every box says what is inside
features: The rest of 30th Celebration's line is on the shelves: Poster Collection (3 packs, plus the Articuno, Zapdos and Moltres promos), Tech Sticker Collection (3 packs, an Alolan Exeggutor or Lucario promo), Binder Collection (5 packs), Mini Tin (2 packs), Knock Out Collection (2 packs and an Eevee promo), and the Sylveon ex and Greninja ex boxes (4 packs each with their foil promo).

Ascended Heroes fills out as well: Tech Sticker Collection (3 packs, a Charmander or Gastly promo), Mini Tin (2 packs), Premium Poster Collection (10 packs, Mega Lucario ex or Mega Gardevoir ex), First Partners Deluxe Pin Collection (5 packs and the Chikorita, Tepig and Totodile promos) and the three Mega ex boxes (4 packs each, with Mega Meganium ex, Mega Emboar ex or Mega Feraligatr ex).

Each of those pack counts and promo lists is taken from the published product copy and marked verified on the product, instead of inheriting the era's bundle/ETB shape. Where a box held one of two promos, neither is listed as guaranteed.
The catalogue is now 542 products, 448 offered and 94 hidden. The only additions are these 14 rows; no existing product's pack count or price changed.

The honest part: the binder and the two mini tins name no promo because a binder, a sticker sheet and an art card are not cards. The promo names are not mapped to catalogue cards, since those promo printings are not in the catalogue, so opening one of these boxes grants no substitute card. The 30th Celebration wrapper is physically six cards while the game deals ten, and the new prices are retail references rather than an official price line.

entries.title: Every modern shelf is sourced
features: The per-product sealed evidence now covers all 95 sold modern rows, not 43. That includes every Mega Evolution set, Ascended Heroes, 30th Celebration and its collections, the modern boosters, and the remaining special sets. Standard products keep their 9/6/36 formats; 30th Celebration's six-card wrappers and 29-pack Ultra-Premium Collections are recorded as physical products.

Each modern Elite Trainer Box now names its real promo: Riolu or Alakazam, Charcadet, Tyrunt, Fennekin, Zarude, N's Zekrom, Kyogre and Nidorina. The 30th Celebration collections name Pikachu ex with Espeon ex or Umbreon ex, plus Ditto, Mew and Mewtwo. Where a promo is named but not catalogued, the box grants no substitute card rather than inventing one.

Two phantom displays are refused now: 151 never had a 36-pack display, and neither did 30th Celebration. Both rows are hidden from the shop, buying, battles, live shows and tournaments while owned stock still resolves; new saves do not seed them. Ascended Heroes' missing six-pack Booster Bundle is now on the shelf.

The catalogue is 528 products, 434 offered and 94 hidden. The 14 hidden modern rows are no-wrapper or phantom rows and are listed separately; there are no sold modern rows left on the generated format.

The honest part: this is a product audit, not a pull-rate audit. 30th Celebration's physical wrapper is six cards while the game deals ten, the UPC's three-card Classic Collection pack is still omitted, and the Mega Evolution promo names do not have mapped catalogue ids. Those are recorded rather than hidden.

entries.title: The shelf says what actually shipped
features: Modern ETBs, bundles and displays now read from a per-product evidence table instead of one era default. The standard Scarlet & Violet line is 9 packs per ETB, 6 per bundle and 36 per display; Crown Zenith's ETB is 10. That covers 43 products across the 2023–2025 sets, with the named ETB promo for each set.

The shop no longer sells a 36-pack Scarlet & Violet—151 display. 151 shipped packs, six-pack bundles, ETBs and collection products, never a standard display; the existing row is hidden for owned stock but cannot be bought or opened from the shop.

Five missing special-set bundles are now on the shelf: Paldean Fates, Shrouded Fable, Prismatic Evolutions, Black Bolt and White Flare each get their six-pack Booster Bundle. 151's bundle was already there.

ETB promos are real where the catalogue holds them. The opener resolves the named card from the promo set — Koraidon or Miraidon for sv1, Snorlax for 151, Lucario VSTAR for Crown Zenith — instead of synthesising an unrelated promo. Where a named promo is not catalogued (Black Bolt and White Flare), the box grants no promo rather than a wrong one.

The honest part: 65 modern rows still use the generated era format because no per-product source was added for them — mostly boosters, the me* releases, and special collections. Their pack counts remain modelled, not verified; reports/sealed-evidence.{json,md} lists every one, and tmp/check-sealed-evidence.ts fails on a count or promo mismatch.

entries.title: Every pack says what is sourced
features: All 522 catalogued product rows — 430 sold and 92 hidden no-wrapper rows — now have a manifest covering pack count, per-pack layout, promos, hit tiers and foil guarantees. Each field carries a source, an inference, a model disclosure or an explicit unverified mark instead of presenting every number as equally certain.

The three General Mills cereal packs and the five 30th Celebration collections have product-level entries. The 30C manifests name the packs, the named promos and the physical six-card wrapper, and the UPC records the three-card Classic Collection pack that this build does not open.

Generic Elite Trainer Boxes no longer imply a real promo. The opener still synthesises one so the box has its beat, but the manifest leaves the promo unverified with no card name; only me6’s published Kyogre promo is named. Bundle, ETB and display pack counts are marked modelled because the catalogue applies one format to a whole product kind.

The manifest is available at /api/shop/products/:productId/manifest and as reports/product-manifests.{json,md}. The report lists every product, every unverified field and the source URLs; tmp/check-product-manifests.ts fails if a product is missing, a field has no status, or an unverified field quietly gains a value.

The honest part: a generic product is still not 1:1. No wrapper photo, box checklist or per-product pull-rate sample was added, so its pack counts and hit tiers remain modelled or inferred; a per-product source is what would promote them to verified.

entries.title: The reverse slot starts in 2002
features: Legendary Collection and Expedition packs now carry their reverse-holo slot. Both sets were being dealt without one because the Wizards branch dropped every reverse slot, even though Legendary Collection is the set that introduced the printing.
Neo Destiny no longer gets a reverse it never had: the rule is now dated to Legendary Collection’s 24 May 2002 release instead of treating every 2002 set as reverse-era.

The 2002 e-Card/EX shape no longer invents a Basic Energy slot in the ten game cards. The game still deals ten where the physical e-Card/EX wrapper held nine; that ten-card abstraction is unchanged, which is why this is a layout correction rather than a claim that every product is now 1:1.

Dragon Vault’s five-card packs now price every card as Holofoil everywhere, not just in the pack estimate. The set is all-foil, but the rare-variant key was reading its plain “Rare” label and valuing the pulls as non-foil.

The honest part: this fixes two reverse-holo sets, not the whole product catalog. The 71 EX/DP/BW sets still use era-typical rates, and bundle, ETB and display products still share the set’s booster table; those need per-product sources before they can be called exact.

entries.title: The paper stays on the card
features: Every identified foil now renders at rest, whether or not Settings → Appearance has advanced foil on. Cosmos, reverse, Cracked Ice, Tinsel, Sheen/Mirror, Water Web, Line, Mirage, Sequin, Confetti and the rest settle at a fixed neutral tilt on the card instead of waiting for the pointer. Named papers used as reverse finishes — POP8 Cracked Ice, the BW Mirror promos, Southern Islands and Best of Game Cosmos — use their own field instead of an empty set reverse.

The switch is advanced foil only. Off keeps the paper and a quiet neutral highlight; on adds the pointer-driven sweep, iridescent colour and embossed relief. Reduced-motion users keep the paper without the movement, and thumbnails below 96 px stay flat so a grid does not pay for invisible canvas work.

The honest part: this is a display change, not new identification. Papers with no researched sheet still render plain foil, unresolved printings still make no claim, and the advanced treatment is still the modelled layer the roadmap describes.

entries.title: Every counter says when it is closed
features: BidBay, Local Deals, Buylist and the Sets gallery now use Pack Shop’s loading, failure and retry pattern. A fetch in flight says what is being loaded; a failed first fetch names what could not load and offers Try again; a failed background refresh leaves the last good screen in place instead of blanking it.

BidBay no longer paints an empty marketplace while its first feed is still arriving. Local Deals waits for both the public board and your own posts before it calls itself loaded. Buylist separates a failed counter from a shop with nothing to buy, and the Sets gallery separates “no sets on file” from “no sets match these filters”.

The honest part: this is the second 13.0 batch, not the whole audit. Forum, Home widgets, Inventory tabs, Market, Notifications, Pack Battles, Settings, Shop subpanels, Storage, Stream, Trade, Wishlist, and the nested Card Shows booth and convention floor still carry the old silent catches or permanent spinners.

entries.title: No more silent screens
features: Achievements, Portfolio, Calendar, Set Detail, Auction House, Card Shows, the convention floor and the Pawn Shop now have Pack Shop's three states. A fetch in flight says what is loading; a failed first fetch says what could not load and offers Try again; a failed background poll leaves the last good screen alone instead of blanking it or spinning forever.

Empty screens now name the next action. A calendar with nothing published points at the convention floor, a set with no cards offers a reload, and the Pawn Shop already separates an empty collection from a search that matched nothing.

The honest part: this is the first batch of 13.0, not the whole audit. BidBay, Local Deals, Buylist, Forum, Home widgets, Inventory tabs, Market, Notifications, Pack Battles, Settings, Shop subpanels, Storage, Stream, Trade, Wishlist, the Sets gallery and the nested booth and floor panels still carry silent catches or permanent spinners and stay on the roadmap.

entries.title: The walls come down
features: The dense screens now speak in labelled lines instead of paragraphs. Storage explains the locker gamble in four rows, Live Shopping names all six room formats, Stream lays out the case-break maths, Pack Shop explains the median sticker, Market labels the per-condition radar, Auction House leads with the room rules, Resale gives ROI its own three lines, Shop breaks rent/mortgage/accounting into rows, and Inventory separates selling, dumping and holding sealed stock.

Nothing about the numbers moved. The pack shelf still uses the median, not the mean; Market still compares each ask with that card’s own condition anchor; dealer sales still pay 70–92% with no fee; the damage dock still pays worn price with no fee; lockers still scrap at about 8¢ on the dollar; and every case-break split is unchanged.

The pass also removed repetition from the Card Shop. Rent, mortgage and the tax treatment of each are three labelled facts instead of one paragraph; walk-ins, ask-versus-market and cross-store moves are three lines under the speed table; and the accountant’s estimates, books and Monday report are separated.

The honest part: this is a copy and layout pass, not a mechanics pass. Every screen still calls the same endpoints and shows the same calculations — only the shape of the explanation changed. Screens that already used one short subtitle were left alone rather than being given a tip list for its own sake.

entries.title: Local Deals stops being a catalogue
features: Local Deals is a seller-thread inbox now, not a Marketplace tile grid. Each row is a person, their listing and the one line that matters — the ask, the risk, or the counter-offer — so the first thing you read is who you would be meeting.

Opening a conversation shows the seller, the listing as an attachment, the cash-only/public-lot rules and one next step: Arrange the meetup or Send an offer. The existing parking-lot meetup, ghosting, counterfeit check, mystery reveals and no-fee cash economy are unchanged.

The seven-venue Deals exit review is complete. Pawn is still the ticket clock, Yard Sales the haggle table, Flea Markets the bins, BidBay the online marketplace, Estate Buyouts the ledger and reveal, and Live Shopping the video room. Local Deals was the one screen still reading like a second BidBay, and it is the one that changed.

The honest part: the conversation list is presentation, not a new messaging system. The seller line is derived from the listing’s existing ask, risk and counter state, and every meetup still runs through the same server calls and outcomes as before.

entries.title: The cards and the roof share a door
features: Storage & Auctions is a mode of Inventory now instead of a second sidebar door. The BUSINESS section is three rows — Inventory, Card Shop and Resale Desk — completing the 32-screen → 17-door consolidation.

Open Inventory and the Inventory / Storage & Auctions tabs sit above the page. Cards keeps every existing view (Raw, Listed, Grading, In Transit, Supplies, Authentication, Sealed); Storage keeps the capacity meters, locker desk, overflow policy, vault rider and delinquent-locker auctions.

Old links keep working: a saved #/storage bookmark, the capacity strip’s “Rent a locker” shortcut and any old feed link open Inventory on the Storage & Auctions tab. The direct route is #/inventory/storage.

The honest part: this is a navigation change, not an economy change. Storage rent, capacity, overflow, scrap floors, vault coverage and locker auctions behave exactly as they did; only the door moved.

entries.title: A box cannot cost less than its packs
features: Bundles, Elite Trainer Boxes, displays and special collections now use the same expected-value floor as boosters: per-pack EV × the number of packs actually in the product. A six-pack bundle is floored at six packs' value, an ETB at nine, a display at thirty-six, and a five-, eight- or twenty-nine-pack special at its own count instead of being treated as a display.

The floor is applied to stored PriceCharting quotes as well, so a real sealed listing below the content value cannot reopen the money printer. The shelf, pack battles, breaks, sealed futures and the dashboard value read the floored quote.
The sealed audit now measures product-level EV, not only booster EV. It reports no offered booster, bundle, ETB, display or special with an expected value more than 1.25× its shelf price.

The honest part: this is raw content EV, with no bulk discount. It can lift an in-print display far above its old MSRP — the point is that the wrapper no longer sells for less than its packs are expected to deal. Variance still lets one box beat the average, and hidden/owned products are not repriced.

entries.title: A pack cannot cost less than its cards
features: In-print boosters now cost the greater of their shelf price and their expected pull value. The ten packs the sealed audit flagged were selling below the cards they deal — Delta Reign at $4.49 against $15.85 of expected value, Phantasmal Flames at $4.49 against $13.41, and Black Bolt and White Flare also in the list — so the shop was handing out a guaranteed profit on every rip. Those prices now start at the pack's own EV.

The floor uses the same weighted pull table as the roller and applies to a stored PriceCharting quote as well, so a real listing below the pack's EV cannot reopen the gap. The Pack Shop, pack battles, sealed futures and the sealed-value figure on the dashboard all read the same quote.

Hidden products are left alone. Their rows exist only so cards and stock already owned still resolve, and repricing a fabricated wrapper at its pull EV would inflate inventory without putting anything honest on the shelf.

The honest part: this is a modelled break-even price, not a claim that a pack is worth exactly that. Variance still lets one rip beat the average, and the estimate moves with card prices. The floor is on boosters; bundle, ETB and display rows keep their existing retail and out-of-print pricing.

entries.title: Every wrapper earns its cards
features: The WotC-era boosters (Base through Legendary Collection, plus the Neo sets) now deal the ten cards their wrapper advertises. They had been reserving a Basic Energy slot their set never printed and, on the 2002 sets, a reverse-holo slot that era never had, so Jungle, Fossil, Team Rocket and the rest quietly handed back nine cards. The energy slot is now only planned when the set actually contains Basic Energy; the 2002 sets get their tenth card back as a common.

Three products now deal the real pack they sold: McDonald's Collection 2021 and 2022 deal four cards (one Confetti holo and three non-holo in the real wrapper), Detective Pikachu deals four (three commons and one rare), and Dragon Vault deals five Holofoil cards. Dragon Vault's whole 21-card set is filed as foil, so any of its cards can appear in the five.

Wrappers that never existed are off the shelf: Pokémon Futsal, the Kalos Starter Set, the four EX Trainer Kits, Pokémon Rumble, Southern Islands, the 2011–2019 McDonald's one-card toys, and the 30th Celebration and Celebrations Classic Collection subsets. Their cards stay in the catalogue and in owned stock; the shop, pack battles and live shows no longer offer a fabricated pack for them.

The honest limits. McDonald's real pack guarantees one Confetti holo, but the catalogue holds one row per card with no holo/non-holo split, so the four cards can all come out non-holo; the guaranteed foil is not modelled. The WotC sets also keep the game's ten-card shape rather than rebuilding the eleven-card 1999 wrapper. And the bundle, ETB and display rows for these small promotions are still the shelf's generic pack multiples, not products those promotions actually sold.

entries.title: The bonus card rides along
features: Shiny Vault (Hidden Fates, Shining Fates), the four Trainer Galleries and Crown Zenith's Galarian Gallery now come inside their host set's booster again — one subset card in the reverse-holo position, with the pack still dealing ten cards. Those cards stopped being purchasable last update when their fake wrappers came off the shelf; this is how a real pack carries them.

The host set keeps its own shape and odds: five commons, the subset card where the reverse holo sat, the rare-or-hit, then three uncommons. The subset card takes that one slot, so it does not add an eleventh card or change the rare slot.

The honest part: one subset card in every host pack is this build's shape, not a measured rate. The galleries are not guaranteed in every real pack, and no source read here gives a per-pack Trainer Gallery or Galarian Gallery figure, so the model deals one every time and the Pack Shop's till says 'Bonus subset' instead of implying odds.
The eight subset-only wrappers stay off the shelf and the Basic Energy set stays unsold; saves rebuild their pull tables once so the host packs pick up the new slot.

entries.title: No wrapper for a subset
features: Eight products are off the shelf: Shiny Vault (Hidden Fates and Shining Fates), the Brilliant Stars, Astral Radiance, Lost Origin and Silver Tempest Trainer Galleries, Crown Zenith's Galarian Gallery, and Scarlet & Violet Energies. Each sold a ten-card booster over a set that only ever came inside another set's packs, so the wrapper could fill one slot and nothing else — the one-card pack the audit found.

Their cards stay in the catalogue and in the game; what goes away is the fake wrapper. Selling a ten-card pack made of nothing but chase cards would have turned a $4 booster into a payout worth hundreds, so there is no honest shape to give these products here. This build does not move those cards into the host set's packs.

Celebrations still sells, and now deals four cards — the size its real booster pack prints — instead of one. Its Classic Collection reprints remain their own product rather than riding along in this one.

The Pack Shop and the pack-battle picker stop offering the eight; stock already sitting in a save still opens exactly as it did. The shop's slot line now shows Celebrations as three rares plus one rare-or-better card.

entries.title: The second parallel earns its hits
features: In Scarlet & Violet packs, Illustration Rares and Special Illustration Rares now come out of the second reverse slot instead of the rare slot. The rare slot keeps its own ladder — Double Rare, Ultra Rare, Hyper Rare, ACE SPEC and the shiny tiers — so a pack can finally show an ex and an illustration rare side by side, and the art card sits in the position a real wrapper prints it in.

The per-card odds did not change, only where the card comes from. An Illustration Rare is still about 1 in 11 packs in the sets that print one, and the Special Illustration Rare keeps its set's own figure: 1 in 32 for 151, 1 in 45 for Prismatic Evolutions, 1 in 40 for Paldean Fates, 1 in 85 for Surging Sparks. The Pack Shop's second-parallel line now prints those rates where it used to say the card was missing from the slot.

Ascended Heroes keeps its measured second slot unchanged: 11.25% Illustration Rare and 1.44% Special Illustration Rare, with the card's own stamp in the rest. Prismatic Evolutions keeps its 5% Master Ball second slot, and the generic art-card rates fill what is left of that slot. One slot holds one card, so a pack cannot show both the Master Ball and an art rare.

The shop's ESTIMATE and the sealed-price anchor follow the move: the second parallel is priced as its own roll, and the rare slot's hit chance is lower by the art-card share, so a pack's expected value stays where it was instead of counting the same card twice. Pull History marks the moved cards as hits, exactly as it did before.

The honest simplification: for Prismatic Evolutions the art-card rates are the era's, not a measurement of that set's second slot — the source that measured the set counted its Master Ball, not its Illustration Rare split. Ascended Heroes is the one set whose art-card slot rates are measured, and it keeps them. Prismatic Evolutions prints no Illustration Rares at all — its 32 art rares are all Special Illustration Rares — so that slot rolls only the SIR (1 in 45), the 5% Master Ball, and otherwise ordinary reverses. Nothing was added to its card list: both Bulbapedia's breakdown and TCGplayer's 1,200-pack study count 32 SIRs and no IRs.

entries.title: Where the cards come from
features: The Pack Shop till now prints the pack's slots for whatever you have picked: how many commons, how many uncommons, the reverse holo or holos, the rare-or-better card, and any Basic Energy or guaranteed classic — with a line saying what fills each one. You can see where a card comes from before you pay for the wrapper.

It is the same plan the roller deals, so the label cannot drift from the pull. A Base Set pack shows its Basic Energy and no reverse holo; Scarlet & Violet shows two parallels with the rarest card last; 30th Celebration shows its guaranteed Pikachu; a set with a second reverse slot says so.

The rare-or-better line carries the real share of packs that upgrade, read from that set's own pull table rather than a rounded profile figure, and names the era's paper — Cosmos, Tinsel, Line, Mirage and so on. A pack whose rare slot never upgrades says that too, instead of implying a hit.

The honest parts. This describes the model's structure, not a guarantee for one physical wrapper: the slot is a rule, and the card inside it is still a draw. Scarlet & Violet's second parallel is labelled as the slot where an Illustration or Special Illustration Rare replaces it in a real pack, which is not what this build deals yet. General Mills mini packs keep their own Sequin odds readout instead of a ten-card breakdown.

entries.title: One paper per era
features: Holo cards are now a small set of generic finishes instead of a per-card research project: plain, holo, reverse holo, Cosmos, Cracked Ice, Tinsel, Mirror, Water Web, Line, Mirage, Starlight, Crosshatch, Confetti and Sequin. Each one points at the sheet the renderer already draws and at the price a pulled copy uses, so a finish is a family of paper rather than a claim about one specific card.

The rare slot now pulls the finish the era actually printed. Base, Jungle and Fossil wear Starlight; Base Set 2 through Call of Legends wear Cosmos; Black & White wears Tinsel; XY wears Mirror; Sun & Moon wears Water Web; Sword & Shield wears Line; Scarlet & Violet wears Mirage. A holo rare therefore comes out as a foil printing and is valued at the foil price — before this, every rare-slot pull was stored as a plain printing, so a holo rare was worth its non-holo counterpart. Scarlet & Violet rares are all foil, as the set itself says.

The odds are the era's, not a guess: the rare slot's plain-versus-foil share comes from the set's own rare split, a hit is always foil, and the reverse slot is always a reverse printing. The coin you see on the odds screen and the card you pull now describe the same finish.

The honest parts. This is a family-level layer: it says a 2004 holo rare wears Cosmos, not which exact sheet that card prints, and the per-card printing database is still what answers a card-by-card question. Cracked Ice, Crosshatch, Confetti and Sequin are registered so a set can roll them, but no set rolls them yet — they need the same per-card evidence the others have before they appear in packs. And the foil itself is still parked behind Settings → Appearance, so the finish decides what a card is and what it is worth, not what it looks like today.

entries.title: The pack, as printed
features: A pack now holds one rare-or-hit card instead of a guaranteed rare plus a separate bonus hit. That second card was the biggest lie in the odds: every pack was quietly richer than the set it came from, and the hit rates on the Odds screen described a slot that sat on top of the rare. The rare slot is the hit slot now — it upgrades at the set's real per-pack odds, and when it does not, you get the plain or holo rare the era actually printed.

Each era's pack has its own shape. Base through Neo Destiny carries a Basic Energy and no reverse holo; Legendary Collection (2002) starts the reverse slot and drops the Energy; Diamond & Pearl through Sword & Shield are five commons, three uncommons, a reverse and the rare; Scarlet & Violet is four commons, three uncommons, two reverse holos and the rare, with the rarest card last. Packs open in the order they are collated, so the reverse holo and the rare sit where they do in a real rip rather than wherever the code felt like putting them.

The reverse slot is now recorded as a reverse printing. It used to be dealt as a plain copy of the card, so the binder and the market valued the reverse holo you pulled at the ordinary card's price. Reverse holos you already own keep the printing they were saved with; new pulls say what they are.

The honest parts. Packs in this game are ten cards, and real ones are not always: WotC packs were eleven with two Energies (one is dropped here), e-Card and EX packs were nine (the tenth card is an extra uncommon), and the Basic Energy and code card in modern packs sit outside the ten game cards, so they are not dealt. Scarlet & Violet's Illustration and Special Illustration Rares replace the second reverse holo in a real pack; here they still come out of the rare slot, which keeps their odds honest but not their slot. And a rare-card Energy — Neo Genesis prints Darkness and Metal Energy at Rare — is no longer mistaken for a second Basic Energy and swapped for bulk.
Shop estimates and sealed prices move with all of this, because they price the same plan the roller deals: a display's expected value no longer counts a hit it was never going to give you.

entries.title: Hammer price, exact
features: An estate lot you can take in full now costs exactly the price the table quotes — the hammer plus the 12% house premium — instead of a few cents under it. The per-card split used to round each card's share before adding the shares back up, which on a large lot came out as much as a dime short.

Nothing changes for a lot the shelf cannot hold: those still charge only the cards that come home, and your cost basis on a full lot now adds up to what left the till rather than a rounded version of it.

entries.title: Foil on standby
features: Card foil is off everywhere: every card now shows its scan flat, at rest and under the pointer, with no reflection, no iridescence and no tilt. The holofoil work had turned into a research project of its own, and the cards are easier to read while it sits still.

Nothing was deleted to do it. The renderer, the printing database, every paper, the audit reports and their checks are all still in the tree, and one switch brings the foil back instantly: Settings → Appearance → Turn card foil on. The choice is remembered per browser.

Honest about what "off" means: this is a display switch, not a removal. Cards keep their identified printing, the binder and market labels still name the paper, and the dev inspector (Shift+H) still draws every layer for anyone poking at the foil system.

entries.title: Plain paper
features: The δ Delta Species holo rares now render on the plain foil they were printed on, not the era's Cosmos sheet. Bulbapedia gives those holos a plain, patternless foil, and the game had been painting them with the starfield paper because it never read the δ marker — which is part of the card's printed name. Fifty holo rares across EX Delta Species, EX Holon Phantoms, EX Crystal Guardians and EX Dragon Frontiers now say so, everywhere they are drawn.
