features: Holo cards are always foil now. Before, the pattern sat at 20% and only came up on hover, so a binder page of holos read as flat art until you pointed at one. The pattern now sits at half strength at rest, with the artwork still legible underneath.

The shine moves by itself. A highlight band sweeps across every foil card every few seconds on a loop, and the delay is staggered per card, so a full binder page glitters unevenly instead of pulsing in lockstep.
Hovering still does something: the foil brightens and the sweep speeds up from 5.5 seconds to 2.2, so the card reacts to the pointer rather than only waking up when touched.
Reduced motion is respected — the foil is still visible, the sweep just holds still instead of looping.
Radiant Collection cards keep their own drawn designs from 0.8.6 and get the same always-on treatment, a little brighter than the rest because the design is the whole point of that subset.

entries.title: The Radiant Collection, card by card
features: Every Radiant Collection card now has its own named foil instead of a shared pattern at a different offset. Pikachu wears the field of big outlined stars it actually has, Jirachi the flowing pink-violet ribbons, and Mew the dense confetti with its green flecks — the three I could check against real cards.

The other 54 follow the same rule: the design is matched to the artwork. Reshiram, Charizard and the Flareons get licking flames; Snivy, Chikorita and Wally get leaves; Piplup and Swirlix get bubbles; Emolga, Dedenne and Elesa get zigzag bolts; Snorunt and Froslass get six-arm snowflakes; Flabébé, Floette, Shaymin and the Floral Crown get blossoms; Gardevoir and Meowstic get orbital rings; Yveltal and Purrloin get spiral galaxies; Audino gets hearts; Altaria and Swablu get cloud puffs; Diancie gets prism bands.

The shapes are real vector geometry — star polygons, bezier ribbons, zigzags, teardrops — drawn per card from the card id, not gradient noise. Each design keeps its own alignment between screenshots and reloads, because the placement is seeded from the id and never from Math.random.
Colours come from the printed foil where I know it: Pikachu's starfield runs pink-red over the yellow card even though Pikachu is Lightning, and Mew's confetti is pink rather than Psychic violet.

Honest about the limits: these are reconstructions from the printed designs, not photographs. Fifteen motifs across 57 cards means a few cards share a motif — they do not share a drawing, because the count, size, angle and placement of every shape is seeded per card, but a Grass card and another Grass card can be recognisably the same family of foil.

entries.title: Every Radiant card, its own foil
features: The Radiant Collection is no longer one pattern with a per-card offset. Each RC card now gets its own composition from a set of six — a fine sparkle field, a ray burst, bokeh, diagonal streaks, glitter crosshatch, and a star field — chosen by hashing the card id, so the subset reads as dozens of different foils rather than dozens of copies of one.

Each card is also tinted by its Pokemon's type: Grass comes out green, Fire orange, Water blue, Psychic violet, Fighting red, Darkness deep purple, Metal steel blue, Fairy pink, Dragon gold, Lightning yellow. The tint comes from the card's own type in the catalog, fetched alongside its rarity, so a Fairy card and a Water card in the same subset do not look related.
Scale and angle are per card as well: the pattern tiles from 0.8x to 1.24x and rotates in 45-degree steps, which is what keeps two cards of the same type from landing on the same grid.
This only changes how the subset draws. Nothing about rarity, value, pulls or prices moved, and every other printing keeps the era pattern it already had.

Honest note, same as before: these are CSS recreations of a foil look, not photographs of the physical cards. Six compositions with per-card tint, scale and angle is a stand-in for the real hand-drawn foils, not a pixel match to any one of them.

entries.title: The whole pattern book
features: Every standard foil pattern is in, mapped the way the printings actually ran: Starlight for Base, Jungle and Fossil; Cosmos from Base Set 2 through Call of Legends; Tinsel for Black and White through Legendary Treasures; Sheen for XY and Generations; Water Web for Sun and Moon through Cosmic Eclipse; Line for Sword and Shield through Crown Zenith; Mirage from Scarlet and Violet onward; and the cracked-ice shard foil for the Trainer Kits.

Pixel/Confetti turned out to be the right answer for two sets I had guessed at: both the McDonald's collections and the Celebrations Classic Collection are printed in the blocky confetti pattern, so the Classic Collection is no longer treated as Cosmos.
Radiant Collection cards now each get their own alignment. Every RC card is foil, and the pattern is seeded from the card id, so no two cards in a binder page sit on the same grid of the pattern.

Reverse holos wear the era's pattern rather than one generic rainbow — a reverse Cosmos card reads as Cosmos through the mask, a reverse Water Web as Water Web — with the artwork window punched out so only the border, frame and text panel catch the light.
Scarlet and Violet made every plain Rare holofoil, so those now show their Mirage foil instead of reading as bulk. Earlier eras keep plain Rares flat, because they were flat.

Still honest about the edges: these are CSS approximations rather than photographs; promotional patterns that never appear in this catalog (General Mills sequin, Play! crosshatch, theme-deck cracked ice on individual cards) cannot be identified from the data; and the first and last sets of each era boundary are approximate.

entries.title: Printings that are their own pattern
features: Some printings are their own foil, and the game now knows it instead of falling back to the era. Radiant Collection — every RC-numbered card in Legendary Treasures and Generations, commons included — wears the RC iridescent confetti, because that subset was foil-only in real life.
Every McDonald's promo set, 2011 through 2022, gets the promo sparkle: larger stars over a warm gold-to-pink sheen, visibly not a normal holo.
25th anniversary: the Celebrations main set carries its ray-burst anniversary foil, and the Celebrations Classic Collection reprints wear the Cosmos foil they were famous for.
30th anniversary: the main set wears the gold confetti anniversary foil, with plain commons left flat because those are not foil in the real packs; the 30th Classic Collection also wears Cosmos.

Where the guess would be a lie, it does not guess. These are still recreations, not photographs, the subset match comes from the catalog's set id and the RC card prefix, and every Classic Collection reprint is treated as Cosmos even though a few of them reprint modern cards whose original foil was different — close beats falsely precise.
Reverse holo still wins over all of it: if the copy in your binder is a reverse holo, that is what you see.

entries.title: Foil on every card
features: The foil now follows a card everywhere it appears. Binder peeks, auction lots, market radar rows, ship bay and storage thumbnails, wishlist cards, trade offers, resale lots and the home rails were still flat because they never handed the renderer a variant — so a thumbnail now resolves its own rarity through a single batched lookup and picks its pattern from that.

One request per screen, not one per tile: visible cards queue for about 40 milliseconds and resolve together, and the answers are cached for the session, so scrolling back through a set costs nothing. A failed lookup leaves the card flat rather than breaking the grid.

Reverse holo stays exact where the game knows the copy. Inventory rows and the pack-opening ceremony pass the real variant, so those show the frame-and-text foil with the art window punched out. A surface that only knows the catalog rarity shows the printing is holo pattern instead, which is the honest answer for a card you do not own a specific copy of.
Foil is decoration and is treated as such: it never touches a price, an odds table or a save, and it degrades to a plain image if the lookup fails or the browser cannot composite the mask.

entries.title: The card in your hand
features: Holo cards look holographic now. Every holo carries the pattern its print run actually used: the Cosmos starfield on Wizards-era holos, the rainbow bar on modern holos, the soft sheen bands of Diamond & Pearl and HGSS, the fine etched crosshatch on Double Rare, Ultra Rare and the V-era cards, the starlight texture on Special Illustration Rares, and the diagonal sparkle on Shiny and Shining printings.

The foil is interactive. Move the pointer across a card and the shine travels with it — the print catches the light at the cursor instead of shimmering on a fixed loop. At rest a card keeps a faint sheen, and it brightens as you hover, so a binder page still reads as cards rather than a row of lamps.

Reverse holo is foiled where the real card is foiled. The art window is masked out, so the light lands on the border, the frame and the text panel and the artwork itself stays flat — which is exactly what lets you tell a reverse holo from a plain holo at a glance.
It shows on the collection grid, set pages, inventory rows, the card detail modal, and both the pack-opening ceremony and its summary; a graded slab keeps the raw card's foil behind the label.

Honest about the fidelity: these are CSS recreations of the patterns, not photographs of real foil, and the design is picked from the card's variant and rarity — holo variants and holo rarities get their era's pattern, and Wizards-era sets are mapped to Cosmos by set id. Surfaces that don't pass a variant or rarity (some thumbnails, market listings) stay flat for now.

entries.title: Every pack, its own odds
features: Booster packs used to guarantee a hit. The ten cards were five commons, three uncommons, a holo rare and a separate "hit" card, and that hit slot always produced something — so every single pack had a rare-or-better in it and a Special Illustration Rare turned up about once in eleven packs. A pack is now the physical ten: four commons, three uncommons, one reverse holo, one rare or holo rare, and a final card that upgrades at the era's real odds or is the pack's bulk. Measured over 500 packs per set: Sun & Moon 18.2% any hit against a 17.6% target, Sword & Shield 26.6% against 29.6%, Surging Sparks 46.6% against 47.3%, 151 46.0% against 44.2%.

The odds are per era and named. Sun & Moon comes from Elite Fourum's 7,020-pack study (GX 11.15%, full art 4.22%, rainbow 1.47%, gold 0.81%); Scarlet & Violet from TCGplayer and Pullmarket community samples (Double Rare ~1 in 5, Ultra ~1 in 9, Illustration Rare ~1 in 11, Hyper Rare ~1 in 100); Wizards-era holo rares are 1 in 3 packs from pokegym's box study. EX, Diamond & Pearl and Black & White have no large public sample, so those three use era-typical estimates and the code says so.

Special Illustration Rare is the tier the hobby argues about most, so the loaded and tight sets get their own numbers: 151 at 1 in 32, Prismatic Evolutions at 1 in 45, Paldean Fates at 1 in 40, Surging Sparks at 1 in 85.

Energy is now one card, never a common. Basic Energy was sitting in the common pool, which is how a pack could hold three of them; it is its own card now, and any Energy at all — special Energy included — is capped at one per pack, with an extra redrawn as bulk. Wizards, EX and Diamond & Pearl packs carry exactly one, as the real ones did; modern packs usually carry none. Across 5,500 simulated packs the highest count seen was one.

Being straight about the limits: The Pokémon Company has never published English pull rates, so every figure here is reconstructed from community sampling, not read off a spec sheet. A set whose catalog has no higher rarity (Base Set has no shinings) gets a zero upgrade chance rather than invented odds, and a gallery-only subset like the Crown Zenith Galarian Gallery still opens as a single card because it has no commons to build a pack from.

The shop's ESTIMATE line and the sealed-box prices now read the same table, so a pack's expected value reflects those odds instead of a flat 1.6× bonus on every hit. Existing saves rebuild their pull tables once on the next launch.

entries.title: The box that was already open
features: Buying sealed product in the Pack Shop with the open-it-now option answered "No sealed product in inventory" every single time. The shop told the server to buy the box and rip all of it in one go, then handed the same box to the opening ceremony — which looked at the shelf and found it already empty. The shop now buys the stock and leaves the tearing to the ceremony: the promo card first, then one wrapper at a time, exactly as it works when you open a box from Inventory.

Nothing was actually lost in the broken version — the packs really did open on the server, the cash left the till, and those cards are sitting in your collection — but you never got to see the reveal. If a purchase ended on that error, the pulls from it are already in your binder.
The packs themselves are untouched: same sets, same pull tables, same prices. Only the hand-off between buying and opening changed.

entries.title: One counter, every screen
features: Fourteen screens were still wearing the old header: a capitals title behind a yellow bar, no mark, and no line telling you what the screen was for. Collection, Portfolio, Grading, Binders, Wishlist, Achievements, Stream, Community, Pack Battles, Auction House, Storage, Settings and Pull History now carry the same counter header as Inventory, Shop and Convention — a mark, a title in sentence case, and its tagline underneath.

Three screens had their emoji stranded inside the title itself. Stream, Auction House and Storage now put the icon where the other screens put theirs, on the left as a badge, and read plainly beside it. Long taglines were left alone: a header that explains what a screen is for is worth two lines.
Presentation only — no price, odd, wage or timer moved in this update. If a screen looks different tonight, it still behaves exactly as it did.

The simulator behind last update's economy numbers also got its clock fixed: it advanced a full day at a time while the game rolls a new game-day every twelve hours, so it charged rent and wages roughly 2.8 times per day. None of that reaches your save, but every simulated cost was inflated; on the corrected clock a satellite that read as barely breaking even actually nets about $45 a day.

entries.title: The premium, checked at the counter
features: The estate house premium was verified end to end against a throwaway copy of the save, and the check found a second bug behind it: a lot larger than your free shelf charged the whole hammer plus premium, then only moved the cards that fit into your binder. You paid for the estate's leftovers. Lots now prorate — the per-card share of the hammer and premium, charged only for the copies that come home — and the activity line says exactly how many stayed behind.

Profit on an estate lot is now measured against what you actually paid for what you actually received, not against the whole box's contents. The earlier version could report a triumphant percentage on a lot where most of the cards never reached you, which is the worst kind of wrong: flattering, plausible, and quietly untrue.

The audit's own recommendations were worth having: the premium itself was correct all along — hammer quoted, 12% on top, the right card art and the right cash leaving the till — but only a runtime check on a real lot could show that the row-level accounting underneath it was lying.

entries.title: The war that nobody wins
features: A price war could only ever end one way: on the calendar. The rival had a fold — the "blinks first" branch that walks its cuts back and costs it reputation — but the condition behind it asked for a till under $25, and wars open with a $60 war chest in the register. A funded rival could not get there in the two to four days a war runs, so in twenty simulated thirty-day campaigns the branch fired exactly zero times out of one hundred and seven wars.

The fold now triggers on the thing that actually happens in a losing fight: the rival has been undercutting you for two game-days, the war has cost it money, and it has won no sales. That is a war worth walking away from. In the same simulation it now folds in about one war in eight, loses two reputation doing it, and the comeback arc runs for the first time — roughly three days of humble, honest pricing before its confidence returns.

The balance holds: most wars still end on the calendar with your nerve rewarded, and the block notices. A rival that folds is a rival that comes back, so winning one is a window rather than a knockout.

entries.title: A shop that pays for itself
features: Satellite shops sold cards at less than a third the rate they should, because the walk-in formula punished margin far harder than it punished gouging. A store charging market × 1.15 — the sane default, since a shop has to make something — got less than a third of the traffic of a store giving cards away, while paying the same rent. The penalty is gentler now (1.55 − price ratio instead of 1.45 − ratio) and the base walk-in rate is up a fifth, so charging a fair margin no longer starves the door.

In thirty-day simulations that change is the difference between a trap and a business: every run used to finish the month down — between $619 and $1,711 in the red — and every run now finishes up, between $462 and $1,096, which is $15–37 a day after rent, wages and manager theft. That lands inside the audit sim's own target of $25–45 a day for a well-run store.

Honest caveat: star managers still do not reliably out-earn cheap ones in these runs. A 5★ manager costs about $16 a day more than a 1★ and the traffic draw is meant to more than cover it, but across nine runs the quality ladder is flat to slightly negative. That is the next thing to tune on this chain, and it is why the sim exists.

entries.title: Which door pays most
features: Every card's detail sheet now answers the question the sell screens never did: of the four ways to turn this card into money, which pays the most? Market listing, buylist counter, instant dealer and pawn counter are lined up side by side with what each actually puts in your pocket, a bar for the share of market value, and how long the money takes.

The numbers are read from the same services that pay them — the dealer's own stable rate, the market's 10% commission, the buylist's best rate, the pawn shop's 40% of fire-sale value — so the comparison cannot drift out of step with what the counters hand over. The panel names the best door and how many dollars you would leave on the table by taking the worst one.

entries.title: Two kinds of lot
features: Estate tables and the resale desk were the same transaction twice: an NPC seller, a lot priced under its contents, pay the ask. Estate tables now charge a 12% house premium on top of the hammer — a liquidation with a clerk and a receipt book, not a private sale. The desk stays fee-free, private and instant. Same bargain, two different deals: the desk is where you move volume, the estate table is where you go for one deep lot and pay the house for it.

The premium is charged at the counter, so the cash check now prices what you actually hand over instead of the number on the tag, and your cost basis includes it — the profit an estate lot reports is the profit you really made. Quoting one number and billing another is what made the old systems feel interchangeable.

Still open on purpose: the sell side has four doors — pawn, buylist, instant dealer and market listing — with fees from 0% to 15%, and nothing tells you which pays best. That overlap needs a comparison the player can see, not another fee tweak.

entries.title: The desk cools down
features: The resale desk was the best money in the game by a distance — a repeatable 26% return every time capital went round, with no risk and no waiting. Sellers now ask more for their lots (52–95% of value for collections, up from 45–85%, and similar lifts for bulk, chases and storage finds), which brings an instant flip down to roughly 18%. Still a good business, no longer the only one worth running.

Satellite shops were a trap: in thirty-day simulations, rent and wages came out over gross in almost every run, so buying a second location lost money while looking like progress. Rent is cut across every tier — the hole-in-the-wall to $4/day, storefront $11, flagship $20, region $46 — and the sim now shows healthy runs turning a profit. Weak managers still lose money, which is the intended lesson, but a competent one can now carry a door.

Honest caveat: the shop fix is a first pass. Rent was the biggest single line I could move without redesigning the sales model, and several simulated runs still finish in the red — the remaining problem is revenue per walk-in, not overhead, and that deserves its own pass rather than another blunt rent cut.

entries.title: Quotes you can trust
features: The dealer's offer on each card is now the offer you actually get. It used to re-roll every time the shelf was read, then roll again when you pressed Sell now, so the number on screen was decoration and reloading was a way to shop for a better price. Each card now keeps one rate for as long as it sits on your shelf — 70–92% of market, fixed until it sells.

Buying a lot you have no room for no longer charges for cards that never arrive. You pay only the prorated ask for the cards that fit on the shelf; the rest stay with the seller and the activity line tells you exactly how many did. Before, a full shelf billed you the whole ask for a partial lot.

Money labels match their arithmetic. The shelf percentage now reads "vs cost" because it is a return on what you paid, not the inbox's edge over an ask; the statement separates dealer proceeds from market profit instead of putting both in a column that looks the same.

entries.title: One desk, everywhere
features: The screens that still wore the default header now wear the desk header: a mark in a rounded chip, the screen's name in title case, and one line saying what the screen is for. Inventory, the Card Shop (both the lease picker and a running shop) and Conventions — floor, booth and the dark-hall screen between shows — are converted. The all-caps titles with the yellow bar were the tell that a screen had no identity of its own.

Tables got two fixes that were making real work harder: action buttons no longer wrap mid-word ("Sell now" was folding onto two lines in every narrow table), and a table's header row now stays pinned while you scroll it, so you no longer lose which column was the dealer offer.

This is the shared shell, not a per-screen redesign — the deals, cards, prices and counters inside these screens behave exactly as before. Plenty of screens still carry the old header; they convert as they get their own pass rather than in one sweep, so nothing gets a new skin it has not earned.

entries.title: The desk gets a statement
features: The Resale Desk is rebuilt around one standing ledger. A tape across the top — capital out, realized, unrealized, ROI — stays put no matter which lane you are in, because "am I actually up?" was the one question the old screen made you open a tab to answer. Lanes are now Inbox, Shelf and Statement, each with its own count.

Seller notes read like notes. Every offer shows a fan of the actual cards, ask against estimated value with an edge bar (the tick in the middle is break-even), and a countdown that turns red inside the last half hour. Looking through the lot is one tap; buying drops you straight onto the shelf with the lot already counted.

The flip table is gone — it was folding "Sell now" onto two lines. The shelf is cards now: real art and names, condition and days held, dealer offer next to its edge, and a banner that tells you what the dealer would pay for the whole shelf today. Stock names and art come with the shelf data itself, so it no longer fires one card lookup per row to print a label.

The Statement lays the money out as labelled rows instead of floating numbers, ending on total ROI with a line explaining what is counted. Honest caveat: the dealer's rate re-rolls every time you load the shelf, so treat the offer as today's quote rather than a price already struck.

entries.title: A bell that actually rings
features: There is a 🔔 in the header now. Deliveries landing, trade offers arriving and other things that want an answer show up there with an unread count, instead of only scrolling past in the activity feed while you are three screens deep in a binder. Click a row to jump straight to the screen that can act on it — a parcel opens your collection, an offer opens the Trading Post — and it marks itself read as it goes.

Deliveries were the worst offender: a parcel could land, get sorted into a binder page, and you would never know until you went looking. Every arrival now badges with the card, how many, who shipped it and how many game-days it spent on the road. Trade offers badge too, because an expired offer is a real loss rather than an inconvenience.

The panel is short on purpose: forty most recent, newest first, 'Mark all read' to clear the badge in one click, and old entries pruned so it never turns into a second activity log. It only badges things that happened after this update — the offers and parcels already waiting in an older save will not appear retroactively.

entries.title: The peek becomes a card
features: Buying a pile at a yard sale now tells you what you bought. The card was already landing in your binder — that part worked — but the only feedback was a toast that scrolled past while the table re-rendered, so a purchase read like nothing happened. Every table buy opens a reveal instead: the card's real art, its name, condition and quantity, paid against what it is actually worth, and the difference. A 10¢ shoebox pile turned out to be a NM Sewaddle worth 29¢ the first time it ran.

The driveway is the one venue where you buy blind, so the reveal is the receipt: it says the pile came off a table, whether you paid the sticker or talked them down, and that the card is in your binder now. Accepted offers open the same reveal as sticker buys — the peek you read on the table is the last thing you see before the card, and the seller's counter no longer ends in a line of text.

entries.title: The parking lot
features: Buying on Local Deals is a meetup now, not a popup. The old flow ended in a one-line dialog — 'X is yours for $20 cash' — which is a receipt, not a transaction with a stranger. It is a scene instead: you pull into the agreed lot under one streetlight, the seller's car already there with the hazards blinking, and the deal plays out in beats — ARRIVE, SMALL TALK, CASH, THE CHECK, DONE. Their line changes with what you bought (a card, a sealed box, a lot), and the narration is yours: counting the money out, taking the item, walking back to the car before the light clicks off.

The corner check is the beat that matters. Cash moves first, exactly like the real thing — then you turn the item over and the verdict lands: genuine, with clean corners and a holo that lines up under the streetlight, or the corner lifting under your thumbnail to reveal wrong stock and wrong gloss. A counterfeit ends the scene standing in the lot holding a fake you already paid for, with the paid-vs-market tally underneath so the damage is in numbers.

The other three outcomes are staged too, because they are the reason a parking lot is a risk. A ghost is an empty lot, one shopping cart, and a message that stays on Read. A card sold out from under you is a buyer already walking away with it and a shrug — 'sorry, sold it locally already.' A counter-offer happens face to face at the car, with Pay or Walk away in front of you instead of a text bubble. Selling your own post still uses the plain receipt, because there is no lot when you are the one being met.

entries.title: The zoom reaches the Trading Post
features: Every card on the Trading Post zooms now. The trader binder grid and the card chips in both sides of an offer were plain images — no preview on hover, and clicking them did nothing — while the same art zoomed and opened the full sheet everywhere else in the game. Both now use the standard card image, so hovering a trader's card pops the enlarged art with its name and clicking it opens the card detail. Verified on the live page: 8 of 8 binder cards and 6 of 6 offer chips armed, the hover preview naming Raikou and Xatu respectively.

entries.title: Real prices, real packs
features: The market wakes up with the in-game day. Price history points, the simulated market and the real re-quote of everything you own or watch now run once per game day — 12 real hours at the default pace, 24 at the slow one — instead of on a 24-hour wall-clock timer that a 12-hour day could outrun. Portfolio values, watchlist alerts and every badge that reads a comp stop being a day stale, and a failed re-quote retries in 30 minutes instead of waiting for tomorrow.

A researched floor under the price model. The comparable model valued collector pieces off the bulk cards they share a name with, which is how Tropical Wind sat at $60 and Ultimate Zone at 13 cents. Fifteen hand-checked values now override inference — Tropical Wind $829, Ultimate Zone $102, Beginning Door $12, Pikachu BW77 $12.84, Aquapolis Porygon $5.90 — each stamped with the month it was researched, so a stale number is visible instead of silent. Bulk that was already right (Sun & Moon basic energies at 20–56 cents) was left alone.

The RGB Mews are chase cards again. 30th Celebration's three phantom secret rares — Mew R, G and B, no set symbol, collector numbers R/RGB — shipped mislabelled as Commons, so they priced like bulk at 86 cents and dealt from the common slot. They are 'RGB Rare' now, carry researched values of roughly $3,450–$3,950 raw NM (late 2026, down from a ~$6,000 October peak), and roll on their own dice at about 1 in 12,000 packs per colour. A display almost never holds one, and the pack shop's chase strip finally names them.

Set completion reads like a dex. Every set in Collection → Sets carries its own bar: how many of that set's cards you own against the total including secret rares, with the set code stamped opposite and the bar going green when the set is finished. A new 'Most complete' sort floats the sets you are closest to closing to the top instead of sorting by release date.

Packs deal their real cards. The rarity ladder only knew about fifteen labels and dropped everything else — Pikachu Rare, LEGEND, Trainer Gallery, ACE SPEC, the shiny tiers — into the common pool; packs were built from Pokémon only, so Trainers and Energy could never appear; and the special slot drew flat, making a Special Illustration Rare exactly as likely as a Double Rare. Every label has its rank now, Trainers and Energy are in the pools, and hits are weighted by real tier odds (SIR ≈ 4.9% against Double Rare ≈ 21%). 30th Celebration packs close on a guaranteed one of the 30 Pikachus — 200 of 200 test packs did — and Classic Collection packs are pure 30-card reprint subset, because that is what the product is. Honest caveat: the game's ten-card packs still include a hit every time, so absolute special rates run about double the real six-card product; the ratios between tiers are what match.

entries.title: The playtest pass
features: 'Fix the four first-ten-minutes bugs.' Three surfaces used to lie to a new player. The convention timer said "0 min of active play" whenever the hall happened to be closed — it now answers from the event calendar, so Home reads 'Weekend Flea Market · Sat 11:00 AM' and Conventions tells you how long until the doors actually open. The Pack Shop had ONE message for three different situations; it now says 'Loading the sealed catalog…' while the fetch is in flight, shows 'Couldn't load the pack shop' with a working Try again if it fails, and only claims it's waiting on a sync when the catalog is genuinely empty. The shop also shows each product's real wrapper art on all 510 rows — falling back to the set's symbol when TCGplayer never listed it — and the rip screen's generic pack art is replaced by the product you actually bought.

'Rewrite the walls of rules text on BidBay, Pawn and Local Deals into short scannable tips.' A new shared TipList turns each monologue into a dialogue-box list of one-line rules — a bold label and a single sentence each, so a first-timer can skim the mechanics of a venue in three seconds instead of reading a paragraph. BidBay's seven rules, the Pawn Shop's valuation notes and Local Deals' venue rules all went through it.

'sweep the rest of the playtest list.' The Pack Shop header no longer nags you to add a PriceCharting token when zero products are priced from real data — it just explains that everything else is derived and badged est. Consecutive '<shop> posted a new want list' lines collapse into one counted row, and a price sync that priced nothing no longer logs '0 cards now priced' into the feed. The weekly digest replaced its twice-printed 'Not enough price history yet' (on a complete 20,641-card catalog) with one honest line explaining that a card needs a week of quotes. BidBay stops showing a fake '0.0★ from 0 sales'. Collection streams pages behind a scroll sentinel — 250 at a time, filling itself the way Inventory does — instead of a 60-card 'Load more' button, and its header now reads '3,750 of 20,641' so a partial list is never mistaken for a full one. An unchanged incoming trade offer reads 'Take their offer' rather than 'Ask for $0.00'.

Pack Battles: the grudge line gets an em dash between the tag and the rematch demand, so 'GRUDGE 7.5 demands rematch: …' reads as a sentence — the rematch pill is nowrap, which used to strand the grudge tag on its own line with nothing between them. Also fixed: Home was firing the activity fetch twice on every mount.

entries.title: Now it looks like a game
features: 'It should be a different UI similar to other Pokémon fangames.' The whole app was reskinned out of dashboard mode into fangame chrome — through the token system, so one palette still restyles all 38 screens. NIGHT (dark, the default): a navy sky with a faint grid, slate panels with bright blue outlines and hard bottom edges. DAY (light): the TCG Pocket blue-to-white wash with white dialogue-box cards outlined in navy ink. The switch lives in the top bar and in Settings → Appearance, persists to localStorage, and flips the first paint. Buttons speak the battle-menu language now: a 2px ink outline, a hard bottom edge that presses down under the cursor, a rounded body — Pokémon yellow for primary, a real red fill for danger, and a new btn-red / btn-orange / btn-green / btn-blue / btn-cyan set for actions that deserve a game button (the rip's 'Tear it open' is red, 'View pull history' is blue). The header is the PKMN LAB bar: a floating rounded bar with a Pokéball drawn in pure CSS — no image asset, so it survives the packaged exe — the screen name as a pill tab, and DAY / CASH / NET WORTH as outlined pill counters like the ₽ money chip; the sidebar carries the same ball over the brand, rounded nav rows with outlined icon wells, and a yellow active pill stamped in ink. Tabs and filter chips became the segmented pill group, tables got zebra rows and a heavier header rule, card tiles lift behind a yellow selector outline on hover, modals and toasts are dialogue boxes, and every screen eases in on route change (opacity only — a transform would make the fading screen the containing block for any position:fixed child).

'Make every menu less cluttered, look way better, and just overhaul the ui to look way cleaner and more like a game.' Button walls collapsed to one action plus a ⋯ menu that names what each choice actually does: the Inventory bulk bar keeps LIST ALL AT MARKET up front and moves Grade / Protect / Reprice / Clear into the menu, every Pack Shop card keeps BUY & OPEN · price and puts keep-sealed plus the 10-pack lot behind ⋯, and the Card Shop box row keeps + Fill with Sell to dealer / Empty in the menu. Search, sort, counts and view controls now ride one toolbar per screen with the browse and density toggles grouped at the right, and the nav itself was regrouped — the deal venues (Pawn / Yard / Flea / Estate / Local / BidBay / Live) got their own DEALS section instead of hiding under MARKET, and Storage & Auctions moved into BUSINESS. A contrast probe walking every text node across 17 routes in BOTH themes at the strict 4.5:1 threshold — sidebar and topbar included — reports zero flags; it earned its keep by catching and driving fixes to the faint greys in both palettes, the light-theme gold and green, the chrome label grey, and links / the day counter onto their own readable blue so the chrome blue could stay dark. tsc and vite build green; the exe was rebuilt with this bundle and passed its headless smoke test (v0.6.0 + SPA).

entries.title: Real packs, real rip
features: 'The packs themselves should have the art of the actual pack so it feels like you are really ripping the pack.' Every sealed product now carries its REAL wrapper art — matched from TCGplayer's sealed catalog (one fetch per set, then only for new sets) and rendered full-size on the tear pack, so you're literally pulling down the top of a Surging Sparks booster. The rip splits the artwork along the tear line: the top strip (with its slice of the real pack) peels away while the bottom half stays in your hand. Products with no catalog listing keep the foil pack they had.

'Card backs should be the official Pokémon card backs.' Every reveal now turns from the official blue-swirl Pokémon TCG card back (bundled into the build — no network needed, works in the packaged exe), replacing the custom TCG LIFE card back. The pack's hue still drives the aura, rays and glow around big pulls.
Pack Battles and Live Shopping inherit the same real pack art through the shared tear component — every rip in the game looks the same.

entries.title: The full ceremony
features: 'Make the animation for opening packs a lot better.' Rebuilt from the foil up. THE PACK: it floats on idle, the shimmer actually drifts, it leans toward your cursor like you're holding it up for inspection, and pulling down drags a glowing tear line through the foil that crackles as it goes — the rip throws 16 sparks and 12 tumbling foil shards that arc out and fall under gravity behind a white flash, instead of a flat pop. THE REVEAL: cards no longer fade in already-face-up. The back swings onto the stage and holds its breath, turns over in 3D (back → front, with the flip swish landing exactly on the turn), then sits with its value while the number counts up and the beat lands — and the timing is tiered, so a $0.12 common is done in 1.3s while a $150+ pull holds a 1.25s pause before it turns and lingers 1.3s after, because the anticipation IS the pull. EPICTY scales with the pull: aura bloom, spinning ray halo, a landing flash and tier-colored card glow (blue/gold/pink/violet) for super/epic/massive/ghost, plus a new whoosh voice in audio.ts distinct from the landing stinger. THE PAYOFF: every landed value counts up (races and settles), hit banners rise in, the summary cells stagger in 42ms apart and the session total counts up too. Skip animation and prefers-reduced-motion still collapse all of it to instant. Verified with tsc and vite build, then live on a scratch copy of the real save: a 60ms DOM sampler recorded the whole stage machine firing on schedule (back 400ms → flip 460ms → value count-up → 480ms beat, repeated across all 7 cards), screenshots of the pack, the flip landing and the summary, and a clean console across three full pack openings.

entries.title: Own the building
features: 'Build the rent-vs-buy decision for the shop: rent that creeps with revenue, or a mortgage line to own the building outright.' Both halves shipped. TENANTS: the landlord now reads the walk-in books every 5 game-days — revenue up 10%+ and rent rises 15%, a 15% slump eases it 8% back toward the tier base, flat books leave it alone — hard-capped at 3× the base so a location can squeeze but never break, and the review lands after the day is quoted so a new rate always bites from the next game-day. The shop header and the Money tab show the live rate, the base, the cap, the crept-from delta and the next review date. OWNERS: the buy card prices the building at 400× base rent (hole-in-the-wall $2,400 · storefront $9,000 · flagship $28,000), 25% down and the rest on a 0.15%/game-day mortgage drafting 0.35% of principal daily — the down payment is principal (never deductible), each draft books a mortgage line in the P&L that tax auto-deducts, and the Today panel swaps the rent roll for the mortgage roll. Because the deed is an asset that cancels its own debt, buying nets to exactly zero on net worth and every payment is pure gain; the mortgage stays out of the unsecured credit line, the interest accrual and the finance panel (extra principal still repays by loan id). Pay the last dollar and the shop reports OWNED OUTRIGHT — $0 rent, no reviews, no drafts, forever. Verified by a 33-check isolated harness (raise/cap/ease/flat/cadence, refused buy leaves cash and the deed untouched, price/down/principal/daily math, drafts with zero stock, P&L + Today rolls + tax deductibility, net-worth neutrality, payoff clears and stops drafting), then end-to-end on the real rig: leased a flagship, saw the crept-from header, clicked Buy (cash −$7,000, net worth unchanged at $117,000), paid $5,000 extra (24% paid, $16,000 left), forced a draft through the live tick (−$73.50, $49.50 of it principal), and paid it off (balance 0, net worth = cash + $28,000 deed), with the P&L reading '🏠 Mortgage 2 entries $-123.58', the tax note 'rent · mortgage · payroll · interest', the day-clock 'Mortgage draft · done · known out -$73.50' and a clean console. Two bugs found and fixed on the way: /api/state 500'd on a save with no shop (the deed query assumed a row — now MAX()), and the day-clock's known-out line printed a literal double dollar sign. tsc, vite build and the reset-trap suite all green.

entries.title: Cash on every row
features: 'Show my current cash next to each battle picker row so affordability is visible at a glance.' Every product row now carries a live you-have line under its stake — the same cash the chip filters against — colored by the comparison: green when the stake fits what you're holding, red with the exact gap when it doesn't (you have $540.00 · short $2.17). Verified on the rig by parsing all 506 rendered rows against their computed colors: zero mismatches in either direction, 145 green at $540 cash — and flipping the affordable-only chip filters to exactly those 145, so the glance, the count, and the chip are one number. The line rides the state poll like the chip label and only sits out while state is still loading. Typecheck and build green, console clean.

entries.title: Only what I can afford
features: 'Add an affordable only chip to the battle picker that hides products whose stake exceeds my current cash.' The picker's chip row gained 💵 Affordable only · under $X — the label reads your live cash off the state poll, and ON the list drops every product whose stake (the same fallback chain the rows display and the sort charges) is more cash than you hold. Verified on the rig: 506 of 506 drops to 148 of 506 at $540 with the maximum visible stake $520.80 and zero rows over; at $2 cash it bottoms out at 0 of 506 and says so — 'Nothing you can afford under $2.00 — flip the chip off to browse the full catalog.' — instead of a silent blank column, and the count chip tracks every state. The chip also disarms what it hides: arm the $151,584 Holon display (rival picked, battle bar live), flip the chip on, and the selection clears so no unaffordable stake sits under the Battle button — the rival stays picked. Typecheck, reset-trap, and build green, console clean across all four states.

entries.title: Employees with lives
features: 'Employees with lives — staff request specific days off, get poached by the rival across the street at 1.2× wage, train up quality stars with experience, and occasionally quit in a huff you have one conversation to defuse.' All four land as one day-keyed life pass over the roster (staffLife gate, pruned like the candidate weeks): every employee now carries mood and xp. Mood drifts daily against the market wage for their stars — underpaid bleeds up to −1/day, fair pay drips back +0.3, premium pay +0.5, a day off actually taken +3, a refused ask −10 and an unanswered one −0.6/day. xp comes from the work itself: a sourced lot 6, a grading submission 8, an attributed register sale 1 — crossing 60/180/380/700 trains a star (📈 in the feed; the wage is untouched, so trained stars are leverage you cash in later). Days off are requested for a SPECIFIC game-day — the next one — and granting one puts them off the clock (buyer/grader skip their tick, the counter drops out of the boost: verified ×1.18 vs ×1.30 with the helper out), refusing costs mood and is remembered. The rival, once open, slips ONE offer at a time at 1.2× wage on a 3-game-day fuse: match, and their wage and payroll ratchet to the offer; let it ride, and they're gone by your hand or by the fuse. And a miserable employee (mood ≤20, chance rising as it falls) files a huff with exactly ONE conversation: hear them out — the raise they named or the day they asked for, mood to 70 — say no, or let the 2-game-day fuse rot, and they walk. Verified on the rig with 46/46 mechanics checks covering every resolve path and both expiries.

The Staff panel is where it lands: three conversation banners in the DemandBanner shape — 💢 the huff with the grievance verbatim and its countdown, ⚖️ the rival offer with match/let-go, 🌴 the named day with grant/refuse — plus per-row XP-to-next-star (0/380 XP to 4★), a mood meter line, an 🏖 off-today badge with off the clock today in the stat line, and a faint market wage under anyone paid less than their stars fetch, so the underpayment that feeds huffs is visible before it erupts. All six paths were clicked through the real panel on the rig — grant, refuse (−10 mood), match (wage ratchets, payroll follows), let them go, hear them out, say no (they walk) — each landing its toast, banner removal, and activity-feed line with a clean console; typecheck, reset-trap, and build green.

entries.title: Affordable first
features: 'Make the battle picker lead with affordable modern products instead of five-figure out-of-print boxes.' Two orderings were lying. The server listed products ORDER BY msrp — which puts out-of-print boxes first within every price tier (the B&W bundle at $5,556 leads every in-print bundle, vintage displays and ETBs ahead of everything in print), and every consumer that renders the list raw inherited it: the stream and break product selects showed exactly that OOP-first order. And the battle picker's 'Sort: Stake low→high' actually sorted by market_price, not the stake it displays and charges. listBattlableProducts now sorts the final list by the real stake, cheapest first, with newest-set tie-breaks — verified on the rig: the raw list and the stream select both lead $4.49 modern boosters, the first row above $2,000 sits at index 258 of 506, and the five-figure vintage displays ($151k) are the last rows in the list. The battle picker sorts by p.stake so the label, the display, and the charge are the same number, with the server's modern-first order preserved inside every price tie. Typecheck and build green, console clean on the rig.

entries.title: The whole box
features: 'In pack battles the packs are wrong — the bundle says 2 packs but there should be 6, the booster display is 36 but you only get 3, and however many are actually in an ETB is not what you get.' The battle ripped a fixed fraction of every product (bundle 2, ETB 3, display 3 — leftover from when stakes were priced as a ripped share) while the products themselves said 6/9/36. Every battle now rips the WHOLE box, per side — the catalog's pack count is the source of truth and the picker prints it ('BUNDLE · both sides rip the whole box — 6 packs a side') — and the stake is the whole product price because that's exactly the cardboard that opens. The per-pack economics are untouched: whole box ÷ every card in it = per-pack price ÷ cards per pack, so cost basis per card is identical to before, pots and grudge doubling scale with the stake, and rival nerve gating grew brackets so ETB-sized stakes sit at nerve − 0.05 and only true whale pots at nerve − 0.2 (grudge rematch locks, kept-pulls, and the decline flavor all unchanged). Verified live on the rig across every size: bundle 6 packs/60 cards/$26.99 in 0.33s, ETB 9/90/$54.99, display 36/360/$161.64 in 0.97s, two full battles driven through the UI with correct verdict math and a clean console.

The same frozen 2/3 counts lived in tournament rounds — the bracket now rips the whole box too (a bundle final opens all 6 packs, the ETB championship all 9), NPC-vs-NPC simulations included, while entries stay the flat $25/$60 and per-card cost basis stays honest. And because a display battle is now 360 cards a side, the card-by-card reveal beat compresses to keep a whole box near a minute of ceremony (measured 471ms/card against the 458ms target) — booster duels keep their original 1.1s cadence untouched, and Skip is always one click away.

entries.title: The lab actually delivers
features: 'Make the Grading page show the reveal ceremony instead of silently discarding grades that resolve during its 20s poll' — that poll hit /api/grading/pending, which resolves due grades server-side and hands each verdict back EXACTLY ONCE, then kept only g.pending and dropped g.revealed. Any grade that came back while you were sitting on the Grading page was destroyed the moment it existed: no ceremony, no toast, nothing — the card simply appeared slabbed in the lists later. (Its sibling endpoint /api/inventory also resolves grades silently, so whichever call reads first spends the verdict — on the Grading page, its own poll was always first, and always the dropper.) The page now asks the lab first, and every fresh verdict is toasted and queued: batch resolutions play one at a time — close the first reveal and the next follows immediately — with a seen-set guard so the 20s re-poll can never re-open a closed ceremony. 'SEE MY COLLECTION' jumps to the Inventory view.

The ceremony itself is now one implementation instead of two: GradeRevealModal and the GRADE_BADGE label map moved to components.tsx, and both Inventory and Grading mount it. Inventory's behavior is preserved exactly — its once-per-verdict guard, the 400ms backdrop open-flush grace, and the tab jump to raw cards all still apply (its previous modal was a nested component; the shared one is top-level, so it also survives the remount audit). Verified live on the rig with forced verdicts: two batched grades pop back-to-back on the Grading page, no reopen across a full poll cycle, the secondary button navigates, Inventory plays the same ceremony on mount, NICE and backdrop both close it, no zombie reopen after reload, console clean, and hover arming intact.

entries.title: The remount audit
features: Follow-up to the Inventory menu fix: every view in the game was audited for the same nested-component remount pattern — components defined inside another component and mounted as JSX get a fresh type identity on every parent render, so React remounts them (and any open state, scroll, focus, or in-flight click) every tick. Two passes were used: a forward scan for nested component definitions and an inverse scan that matches every capitalized JSX mount against its definition site, across App, components, and all view files. The only other offender was the Pack Battles rip ceremony: its two pull columns were a nested component that remounted both sides every ~1.1 seconds while the auto-play cadence advanced — the card tiles rebuilt under the cursor each beat, image loads restarted, and clicks on a card to inspect it mid-animation could land on a node that had just been swapped out. The columns are now direct render calls with stable DOM for the whole ceremony. Everything else in the codebase already mounts nested-free (the nine Inventory pickers were fixed in 0.5.89); the inverse audit reports zero remaining nested mounts, and typecheck, reset-trap, and build are green.

entries.title: Menus that stay put
features: 'The grading menu in inventory keeps closing' — every picker in Inventory (⚖ Grade, 🛡 Auth, protect, bulk grade/reprice/protect, the grading reveal) was a component defined INSIDE the view, so its type identity changed on every re-render: React remounted an open menu every time the state poll landed, rebuilding the DOM under the cursor. In-flight clicks were dropped on the old node, scroll position and mid-submit progress reset, and — worst — an impatient second click racing the open-flush landed on the backdrop that had just appeared and bounced the menu shut the instant it opened, which is exactly the open-close flicker that made the menu feel like it kept closing and re-opening. The modals are now stable render calls (same DOM node across polls — verified by stamping an open menu's backdrop and watching it survive consecutive state ticks), the bulk-submit progress and reprice slider moved up into the view so they persist through a poll, and every backdrop close now runs through a 400ms grace window that ignores the tail of the opening gesture — a double-click can no longer close what it just opened, while ordinary backdrop clicks still close normally.

The grading reveal ceremony got the same once-only discipline the auth ceremony already has: it now pops exactly once per verdict (guarded by inventory id) no matter how many times Inventory's load() runs after actions, and it asks the lab for reveals BEFORE /api/inventory resolves them away — previously that call spent the verdict first, so the ceremony only fired in a race window and re-armed unpredictably otherwise. Typecheck and reset-trap green; verified live on the rig — menus hold through polls, backdrop close works outside the grace window, bulk grade modal opens with state intact, and no console errors from the new bundle.

entries.title: Hover comes to the inventory — and the tick that finally sleeps
features: 'Card hover should work in the inventory' — it worked in every other view but this one: SlabCard never forwarded the card id to its image renders, so without an id CardImg never armed the zoom. SlabCard now passes cardId to BOTH of its renders (the raw fallback and the slab well), and all three inventory call sites hand it the row's card id — so the flat table, By-set group rows, the comfortable VirtualGrid cells, and list density all get the same hover-to-zoom preview and click-to-open card modal as the rest of the app. Verified across all four surfaces on the rig: thumbs armed (100/100 flat, 200/200 By-set, 200/200 list, 200/200 VirtualGrid), enter shows the preview with the card name, leave clears it, click opens the modal, Escape closes it.

While verifying on a big rig save (3.7M price records) the server turned out to be hiding three real bugs — two silent perf/data killers and one that could wedge it entirely. RESALE DEALS DIED ON ARRIVAL: ensureOpenDeal wrote expires_at in SQLite's datetime format ('2026-10-03 20:26') while every reader compares against ISO ('2026-10-03T20:26:00.000Z') — same-day string comparison puts the space before the 'T', so every deal was already expired the tick it was created. The resale inbox never filled, and because no open deal survived, nearly every /api/state re-ran sampleLotCards's ORDER BY RANDOM() join across 3.7M price records (1.1s of sync CPU per poll). The same bug truncated sponsor offers at UTC midnight (a '48h' offer never saw day two); both writers now stamp ISO. SAVE BACKUPS COULD STACK AND WEDGE THE SERVER: the day-key is only marked after a backup resolves, so while one was starved the 20s tick spawned another snapshot every pass — each stacked pass re-inspecting every file in the directory with 5s busy timeouts (0-byte torn files each threw 'no such table'), driving the event loop to 99% CPU inside inspectSnapshot until the server stopped answering. snapshot() now holds a single in-flight promise (concurrent callers queue onto one copy — two simultaneous manual backups serialize and both succeed), inspect rejects torn files by size before sqlite ever opens them and gives locked files a 250ms busy timeout instead of 5s, and prune is stat-only so a piled-up directory can't turn keep-3 into hundreds of sqlite opens — torn residue is dropped first so it can never squat a keep slot. The backup itself now copies 1024 pages per event-loop turn instead of better-sqlite3's 100: a 639MB stress save snapshots end-to-end in ~5.6 seconds under live browser load (it was 7.5 minutes and still going), with cash/inventory verified in the response and keep-3 prune holding. THE 2.6-SECOND TICK: every latest-price lookup pins card_id+kind and needs rows newest-first, but idx_prices_lookup has variant sitting between kind and retrieved_at — so search, auction-lot spawning and friends paid a per-card temp B-tree across millions of rows on every call, as synchronous CPU inside request handlers. New covering index idx_prices_latest (card_id, kind, retrieved_at DESC, market): cards search 2.6s → 190ms, auction-lot spawn 2.9s → 170ms, /api/state 9-21s → 0.5-3s under the same live load. Reset-trap and typecheck all green.

entries.title: Absolutely everything resets
features: 'The PSA special didn't reset upon reset' — correct, and it was the symptom of a wipe that only ever knew about the tables it had been told about. THE ROOT CAUSE: the reset wiped meta with a BLACKLIST of keys, and psarush:state (the whole live event — quota used, backlog, end time) simply wasn't on it, so the special survived a fresh start. Meta is now wiped by KEEP-LIST instead: every key that is not config (sync checkpoints, API quotas, price pipelines, feed cadence, migration stamps, UI prefs — 27 keys on the live save) is deleted, so state keys added by any future feature can never outlive a reset again. The live save went 91 meta keys → 27, psarush:state/npcWave/rolled/drainDay included.

The wipe itself grew from ~46 tables to 97 — everything except the card database (sets, cards, prices, pack products) and the config layer (settings table: API keys, day length). Newly wiped: the PSA rush and every event/world feed (flea markets, live shows, card shows, forum, incoming deliveries, reprint shocks, market digests), the player's businesses and holdings (shop + cases/consignments/ledger, franchise + managers, storage units and the cards inside them — those used to survive as ghost rows pointing at deleted inventory — lockers, vault policy, bulk boxes, grab bags, supplies), money records (bank loans, finance credit score back to 600, tax filings/payments, sales-tax remittances, net-worth history, achievements), eBay shipments, sealed-futures loans, buylist wants, rival shop/cases/sales, estate buyout listings, and the set-demand cohort oscillators. Table deletes are existence-checked (a save predating a feature must not break reset), the wipe keeps the child-before-parent discipline everywhere, and the Settings confirm now says exactly what happens. The trap regression test grew with it: 97 tables seeded and asserted zero, meta keep-list equality, finance re-seeded to defaults, the armed pawn trap proving the old order throws, and double-run idempotence. Verified end-to-end on a copy of the live save: HTTP reset returns ok, every table to zero, meta down to the 27 keepers, cash $1,000, day 1.

entries.title: Reset, for real this time
features: 'Cash did not reset when resetting save' — hunted down and fixed, plus two more reset bugs found along the way. THE FAILING CHAIN: the wipe deleted pawn_shelf and pawn_loans AFTER the big early `DELETE FROM inventory`, but pawn_loans.inventory_id references inventory without a cascade — so on any save with an open pawn loan (or a ticket on the shelf) that delete threw FOREIGN KEY, the one-transaction wipe rolled back completely, and the save came back untouched: cash the same, day counter un-stamped, everything else intact. The chain now goes shelf → loans → inventory, all before the inventory wipe, and the loan-book tables' own parent/child order is corrected too. SECOND BUG: the wipe cleared resale_deal_cards but never resale_deals itself, so deal rows survived every reset as dead 'open' listings. THIRD: failure was silent — the endpoint 500ed with a bare FK error and the client toasted a generic 'see the server log'; the wipe now lives in server/services/savereset.ts with every statement annotated, so the endpoint returns the exact statement that broke ('reset stopped at "DELETE FROM yard_sales" — … — nothing was changed'), the server logs it under [reset-save], and Settings shows the real message instead of swallowing it. One retry rides along for a transient busy/locked file. Verified three ways: the new trap-save regression test (server/scripts/reset-trap.ts — seeds every child-before-parent chain the wipe touches, proves the OLD order throws on the armed trap, then resetSave commits: 44 wiped tables at zero, cash $1,000, day-1 stamps, one Main Collection binder, card database and authDiscountPct untouched, second run idempotent), a forced mid-wipe failure against a copy of the live save (annotated 500, rollback proven — cash and created_at unchanged), and the live-save reset itself (pawn chain included) landing on $1,000/day 1.

Ship-time data loss guard, same family of bug — and it caught a real loss: the backup that actually runs (build-exe.sh step 5, before `rm -rf release`) copied only tcglife.db, but taskkill -F never runs a clean SQLite close, so since the last checkpoint everything the player did lives only in tcglife.db-wal — the main-file-only cp archived a stale image and the rm then destroyed the WAL with it (this ship cost one session's world-state: NPC auction/flea seeds only — cash, collection, and the day counter were identical on both sides, and the daily gates re-arm on the next boot's catch-up tick). Both backup sites now fold the WAL into the main file with wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) first (refusing to back up if the fold fails) and carry any WAL/SHM residue alongside so a restore can put it back.

entries.title: The line, live on your dashboard
features: The PSA rush is now interactive from the Home dashboard: while the special runs, a live event card sits right under the KPIs — a per-second countdown to the doors closing, the slab-premium badge (decaying as the quota fills), and the quota rendered as a two-tone race bar: the NPC horde's share in red, yours in yellow, with the split spelled out ('23/40 · 4 yours · 19 eaten by the scene') plus slots-left and the current queue drag. The 🏷 Rush-eligible cards button drops you on Grading pre-filtered to the cards the $10 line is the play for — a one-shot store flag so the destination view lands with the filter already on, and the same filter stays available as a manual chip on Grading ('rush-eligible ✓', with quota telemetry in its tooltip) that toggles between the full candidate list and the special-only picks. To make 'rush-eligible' mean something, the advice engine now lets the open special join the best-service comparison: the $10 tier was invisible to candidates before (the list only knew the three standard services and refused anything under $15), so the rush's actual sweet spot — $8–15 raw cardboard — never appeared. During a rush the candidates pool floor drops to the special's minimum and every card weighs the line against standard/express/premium; grails still route to express/premium where the grade bias earns it. Verified on the rig: Home card with live countdown and quota bar, shortcut → Grading landing pre-filtered (7 of 8 candidates, express grail excluded), and the chip toggling back to 8 of 8.

Ride-along: /api/grading/rush now carries minRawValue (the special's raw floor) so every surface agrees on what 'eligible' means, and the generic .bar/.fill/.mt4 styles exist at last — the grade-distribution bars, shop bin stock bars, and any progress track were rendering invisible because those rules only existed scoped to .syncbar.

entries.title: The scene has taste
features: Roadmap line 148 (macro six): population & meta drift — the scene itself changes over months. Three engines share one module (demographics.ts). POPULATION: each era carries a slow mean-reverting taste multiplier (0.82–1.35) walked once per game-day, with a permanent hold-forever creep on vintage — as the old guard's era climbs, vintage prices rise while vintage SUPPLY thins (the marketplace feed thins vintage lots by eraSupply, feed never starves, composition just shifts to newer cardboard). META BOOMS: every game-day the hobby may catch fire — a pop star's Charizard photo, a viral nostalgia rewatch, the chase hit going viral on card-Tok — lifting an era's demand 8–26% at peak (chase cards catch the full wave, bulk rides along at 40%) for 6–16 game-days with decay through the life, spawn and cool lines in the feed. SET DEMAND PROFILES: every set's long-term value profile (chase vs bulk) emerges from two SIMULATED collector cohorts instead of a fixed curve — chase hunters on a ~57 game-day rhythm and set completists on ~89, each set with its own phase, walked daily toward their oscillators with noise into set_demand (demand/tilt/trend). Cards price through regimes.factor as pop × boom × (chase/mean or build/mean), so a set's chase-vs-bulk split is a living thing; out-of-print sealed curves scale by the same demand (0.65 chase/0.35 bulk — rip vehicles track the hits) while in-print product stays at retail. The Market view gains a scene strip: live boom headlines with peak/decay countdown, era taste chips (vintage says so when supply is thinning), and hottest/coldest sets by demand with trend arrows. Verified on the rig (35/35): the walk's bounds and day guard, boom spawn/expiry with chase reacting harder than bulk, exact factor composition, OOP scaling vs in-print retail, supply thinning with the feed fallback, and cohort evolution math.

Ride-along: estimates.ts now exports eraOf/Era as the single definition of vintage/mid/modern the scene shares, and /api/market/scene serves the strip alongside the existing regime and seasonal endpoints.

entries.title: The futures desk opens
features: Roadmap line 150: the secondary market for sealed. Sealed boxes now trade like commodities and condition is the whole spread. Every lot carries a condition — buys stamp case-fresh, and fresh units trade ABOVE market (+10%) while worn trade BELOW (−10%), with the spread decaying to ±2% by two years out of print (on vintage boxes survivorship is already in the comp). Shelf wear is real: 8% per game-day a fresh lot slips a grade (escrowed collateral is immune — the vault doesn't scuff), so the premium is a perishable asset. The damage dock is worn stock's second chance: re-wrap for 10% of unit value and the crew hands you a fresh box at your original basis, or dump worn stock at its worn price (the 10% dealer fee rides inside). The loan desk lends against sealed inventory the way banks lend against gold: post units as collateral (they move to the vault — no ripping, no selling, tagged escrow), borrow up to 60% of their WORN value at 0.6%/game-day compounded with no fixed term, redeem units early at pro-rata principal, settle in full, or walk away — the bank keeps the boxes, sells them at the dock, and mails any surplus. When the unpaid balance outgrows the boxes (135% overhang) the whole ticket re-prices to 0.9%/game-day with a warning logged. The Inventory sealed tab is rebuilt around the desk: a futures explainer, the loan-desk panel with active tickets (redeem input, settle, forfeit), Fresh/Worn price columns with per-row P&L, worn ×N and 🏦 vault ×N badges, and POST ALL. Every dollar sits on the books: net worth prices sealed at condition and subtracts loan balances, insurance appraises at condition, and rip/sell all refuse escrowed stock with a pointer to the desk. Along the way one shipped-bug fix: posting mixed fresh+worn stock as collateral no longer merges it into one mislabeled vault lot — escrow keeps one lot per condition, and redeem/settle hand every box home in the condition it was posted in.

Ride-along: the sealed sell endpoint is condition-aware (SELL FRESH / DUMP buttons target their grade), /api/pulls/summary reports sealed per condition, and the state payload's sealed value and debt figures run through the same futures math as the ledger.

entries.title: Everyone's in the line
features: The PSA rush is now a race. Once per game-day during an active special, an NPC wave joins the queue — Marcus, Buylist Betty, Parking-lot Paul, Denise, the Discord mod, and the rest of the named scene, growing daily as word spreads (day N: ~3N±2 slots) — and they eat REAL quota plus add to the very backlog the player waits in. Feed chatter logs each wave with named collectors, remaining slots, and the current queue cost, and the banner telemetry splits the quota: '23/40 used · 4 yours' makes the race legible, with 'quota GONE — the scene ate the line' when the horde wins. The slab premium is now a genuine supply curve instead of a toggle: it decays linearly from +12% toward the +6% hangover floor as the quota fills (the line IS the incoming slab supply), and through the backlog hangover it fades from +6% to nothing as the queue drains. Along the way two shipped-bug fixes: the backlog multiplier (0.5 game-days per submission, as the 0.5.81 changelog already advertised) is now actually applied to quoted turnarounds and wave chatter, and the hangover drain is guarded per game-day instead of per 15-second tick (a rush ending while you slept no longer clears the queue instantly). Verified on the rig (14/14): wave sizing and daily escalation, quota exhaustion by NPCs alone, one-wave-per-day guard, premium decay curve and hangover fade, drain guard, and the banner telemetry.
Ride-along: back-log chatter and banner queue figures now share one backlogDelayDays() source of truth.

entries.title: The lines go around the block
features: Roadmap line 136: grading pediment events. The 🏷️ PSA special spawns at random (~6% per game-day when idle — unlike the fixed seasonal calendar, the lab does what it wants) and runs 4–7 days. During the rush: a $10-per-card special tier appears in the Grading service list (min raw $8 — even bulk gets a shot at cardboard immortality), every submission's turnaround inflates by a live backlog counter (0.5 game-days per submission, capped at 20 — quoted ETAs across ALL services shift, and the Grading banner spells out the queue's cost), a 40-slot quota rations the special (a 'only N slots left' warning at 10, and at 0 the tier vanishes and the line is announced cut), and graded cards price at a +12% slab premium on every pricing surface that reads gradedPriceOf — live comps and estimated fallbacks alike. When the rush ends the party doesn't: a backlog hangover keeps turnaround dead and slabs at +6% while the queue drains 2 submissions per game-day. Two plays, both mechanical: submit cheap into the quota and eat the wait, or hold slabs and sell into the premium while the lab grinds. Verified on the rig: idle neutrality, spawn roll, special pricing/turnaround, quota burn + backlog growth on submission, standard-tier submissions inheriting the delay (measured in game-days), premium flowing through gradedPriceOf, quota exhaustion hiding the tier, and hangover premium/drain. Grading view carries the live banner (special state, quota, premium, queue, arbitrage explainer) and /api/grading/rush exposes the section.
Ride-along: listServices() and submitForGrading() now share the rush-adjusted turnaround math (previously the quoted days and the actual due-date math could drift once events touched either).

entries.title: The agents clock in
features: Roadmap line: wishlist agents & price sniping. Arm any wishlisted card with a 🤖 standing auto-buy: a per-card price cap (defaulting to the card's 🔔 alert target if you've set one) and an exact condition (NM/LP/MP). Once per game-day the overnight sweep walks the buy surfaces — marketplace feed listings and BidBay single lots — and auto-buys the cheapest qualifying lot at or under cap, debiting cash, consuming the listing, scheduling the delivery on the game clock (exact same pipeline as a hand buy: market vias ride the market feed, BidBay vias ride ebay), and logging one 🤖 activity line with the seller, price, cap, and ETA. Discipline rails: a global per-order cash cap (default $250, adjustable $1–$50k, GET/POST /api/wishlist/agents/cap) bounds every single buy AND the whole sweep's budget — one sweep spends at most the cap; one buy per agent per sweep; vault shelf checks honored (a full shelf refuses the buy, same as a hand buy); agents buy LISTED lots only and never pay distributor market price; validation refuses arming without a cap, sub-$0.50 caps, off-whitelist conditions, and non-wishlisted cards. UI: the Wishlist header gains the agents line (N on duty · cap/order), a 🤖 Sweep now button, a 💵 Cash cap editor, an On-duty panel with per-agent badges, and per-row 🤖 Arm/ON buttons in both densities (armed rows show the green 'Auto-buy NM at ≤ $X — sweeps once a game-day' line). Verified on the rig: 18/18 scenario checks (arm guards, market buy with exact total/cash/delivery, sweep idempotence, per-order cap blocking an over-cap BidBay lot, cap raise letting it through, ebay via on delivery, disarm) plus the once-per-game-day tick guard (second tick same day is a no-op) and the full UI pass.

Ride-along: the Wishlist view now loads its agents panel through the same load() (no stale state after arming/disarming), and the wishlist API response carries the agent fields so both list densities render armed state without a second fetch.

entries.title: The community scene
entries.fix: Waiting-verdict badges so lab results are never missed now that reveals don't auto-pop: /api/state gained a counters object (arrived auth tickets + finished grading jobs), the sidebar's Inventory row shows a yellow badge with the combined total, and the 🛡 Authentication / Grading tab chips badge their own remaining counts. Updates ride the existing 15-second state poll — no new endpoint. Verified on the rig: sidebar badge shows the combined total while off-view, in-view chips show their per-tab counts on the state tick, and mid-session verdicts badge the chips without any modal ambush.
entries.fix2: Fixed the authentication panel's reopen loop: with more than one lab verdict waiting, the arrived-verdict reveal modal popped again immediately after every Close — the auto-pop lived inside the view's load(), and arrived tickets stay listed in /api/auth until a reveal spends them, so each refresh found the next ticket and re-opened a modal mid-action. The verdict-landed-while-you-were-away ceremony now runs once on view mount only; additional waiting verdicts surface as manual 🟢 'Open the envelope' reveals from the 🛡 Authentication tab's in-lab list, which already existed. Verified on the rig with two arrived tickets: one ceremony pop on mount, Close keeps it closed, the second reveals manually and stays closed.
features: Roadmap line 146 is live: the positive half of the social layer. The 🫂 Community forum carries a 0–100 standing score you earn three ways — post a pull from your collection (the room prices pulls by story, not market: warmth 1–5🔥 scales with cost basis and favorites flex harder), answer newbie questions (3 per game-day, +1 each), and write a guide (1 per game-day, +1+warmth from the guide pool). Standing unlocks real privileges around town: at 10, group-buys (co-fund one of four board cards — Lugia, Beauty, Charizard, Typhlosion — with 3–6 collectors, your share debited up front, the card lands in your binder on the game clock at the FULL lot basis, one buy in flight at a time, organizing one earns standing too); at 25, estate first-refusal (when an estate listing is about to spawn, the heirs DM you first — one DM per game-day, a 1-game-day exclusive window before everyone else sees the board); at 40, ship-first trade trust (Trading Post partners mail their card before you mail yours — mechanically a +2 effective trader-reputation floor, the escrow anxiety ends). The street bleeds in: while a scam-accusation suspicion flag is up, ALL forum rep gains halve and the forum shows a red warning that it reads the gossip. Tiers run lurker → regular → known → trusted → pillar with unlock toasts at each perk threshold; the view shows the rep meter with a next-perk marker, the perk ladder with OPEN states, the group-buy board with in-flight lots and ETAs, and the thread feed. Server: forum_posts + forum_groupbuys tables, /api/forum (+ pull/reply/guide/groupbuy), forumTick rides the market tick chain for deliveries, estatebuyout spawnSale feeds offerFirstRefusal, and trading.ts reads the rep meta directly (no import cycle). Also in this build: every sidebar tab is now always visible — locked ones render as their own 🔒 row with the exact unlock requirement, live progress (cur/goal), and the click-through lock toast, instead of one collapsed hint per section. Verified on the rig: reply cap + rep ladder, halved gains while hot (3→3.8 pull) and full after clear, group-buy refusal at rep 5, share debit, one-at-a-time guard, forced-due delivery at full-lot basis (125 lot / 125 basis), refusal metas + window scope + one-DM-per-day, ship-first flag at 40, pillar tier, rep cap at 100, and cross-connection /api/forum visibility; UI pass confirmed the nav rows and the Community view end-to-end.

Completion pass on the same build (found by auditing the feature end-to-end): estate first-refusal is now real instead of just a DM — /api/estate-sales listings carry a `refusal` flag during the window (gated at rep 25, scoped to the DM'd lot, and cleared with the metas by the estate tick once the sale is bought, taken, or expired), the Estate board shows a 📩 first-refusal banner on that listing, and the heirs' negotiation floor softens by 4 points while they hold the lot for you. Ship-first's rep read dropped its once-per-process cache — a cached value would have pinned the perk to rep-at-boot until relaunch; every proposeTrade now reads forum:rep fresh. The unused held_for_groupbuy inventory column was dropped before it ever reached a schema-fresh install. Verified on the rig: refusal flag false at rep 24, true only on the DM'd listing at 25, false again after clearing, and the banner rendering on the Delgado heirs' panel.

entries.title: One slider, a hundred asks
features: Bulk repricing — the last bulk action the selection bar couldn't do. Pick any cards and the ↻ REPRICE button opens a nudge modal: a ±50% slider with −25/−10/−5/+5/+10/+25 presets, a live asking-total preview (before → after) and a cost-basis check that warns how many picked cards would dip under their own basis at this nudge.
